entries.title: Ratchet: How Reliable Must an LLM Judge Be to Retire a Skill?
entries.summary: Paper on self-evolving agent skill libraries. Proves an exact reliability threshold for the LLM judge that governs skill eviction: if the judge's rate of scoring failures as passes reaches (1-tau)/2 for eviction margin tau, no eviction happens at any sample size. Reports that unmaintained libraries drift until adding a new skill scores worse than adding nothing, and that LLM-written skills contribute 0.0pp over a no-skill control vs. +16.2pp for human-written skills. Their Ratchet method (per-skill contribution eviction, library-width cap C, constrained synthesis) lifts held-out pass@1 by +0.328 on a hard MBPP+ slice. Amazon Science open-source code.
entries.takeaway: In self-editing agent skill libraries, the judge's false-pass rate (not its overall accuracy) determines whether eviction can ever converge; asymmetric judge errors are the bottleneck, and end-task score is a poor alarm.

lessons.point: There is an exact non-convergence threshold on the judge: above a false-pass rate of (1-tau)/2 for eviction margin tau, no sample size can ever retire a skill.
lessons.excerpt: a judge scoring failures as passes at rate $(1-\tau)/2$ or above retires nothing, at any sample size, for eviction margin $\tau$.

lessons.point: Empirically, LLM-written skills in an audited system contribute nothing over a no-skill baseline, while human-written skills contribute meaningfully; unmaintained libraries drift negative.
lessons.excerpt: LLM-written skills are worth $+0.0$percentage points (pp) against a no-skill control, human-written ones $+16.2$pp. Unmaintained, a library enters \emph{library drift}, growing until injecting a skill scores worse than injecting nothing.

lessons.point: The two judge error directions are not interchangeable: false-negatives cost sample efficiency (recoverable with more trials), false-positives displace the eviction statistic irrecoverably.
lessons.excerpt: Passes scored as failures cost sample efficiency, which more trials buy back; failures scored as passes displace the eviction statistic, and no correction inside the rule recovers it.

lessons.point: End-task score is a bad early-warning signal for library drift; it moves at most a fifth of the governed lift and not monotonically in the judge's error rate.
lessons.excerpt: End-task score is a poor alarm, moving by at most a fifth of the governed lift and not monotonically in the rate.

actionable.title: Add a false-pass-rate gate to any self-editing agent skill library
actionable.detail: For any agent stack where an LLM judge decides which auto-generated skills to keep (Voyager-style memory, Claude 'skills', self-evolving toolboxes), measure the judge's false-pass rate offline against a calibrated set. If it exceeds ~(1-tau)/2 for the eviction margin you use, skills never get retired regardless of sample size — the library grows and drifts. Monitor library drift via per-skill contribution over a no-skill control rather than end-task score, which the paper shows is an insensitive and non-monotonic alarm.

entries.prior_art: Related to Voyager-style skill libraries, self-refinement literature, LLM-as-judge calibration (Zheng et al. MT-Bench), and control-theory-style bounds on noisy estimators.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b011-2.txt (LaTeX math retained as-is in excerpts). Related claims exist in ledger. Novelty is meaningful because the exact false-pass threshold and the asymmetry between judge error directions is a specific quantitative claim; relevance capped mid-range because scope is skill-library curation, not general production agent security.

entries.title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
entries.summary: A within-record audit across five API models and six countries tests whether LLMs still redirect their forecasts when they know a country label was assigned uniformly at random. Verified metadata materially lowered Brier loss (-0.040), but disclosing that a label was random did not reliably attenuate its influence — models absorbed the spurious cue anyway.
entries.takeaway: Telling the model 'this cue is random, ignore it' does not actually get it to ignore the cue; treat metadata channels as load-bearing even when your prompt says they aren't.

lessons.point: Opaque country labels and disclosed-random country labels produced identical country-direction shifts (0.214 each), and paired attenuation was essentially zero (0.0003, 95% CI includes zero).
lessons.excerpt: opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166])

lessons.point: Verified survey-country metadata was genuinely informative: it lowered Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while the random-label regret CI included zero.
lessons.excerpt: Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero

actionable.title: Don't rely on 'this field is random' disclaimers in prompts
actionable.detail: When context contains fields that may or may not be authoritative, in-prompt disclosure of 'this is random, ignore it' fails to attenuate uptake; instead, remove the field, mask it, or route through a separate LLM call that never sees it. Verify with a within-record swap: same prompt, real vs. randomized field, measure directional drift.

entries.prior_art: Broader work on LLM sensitivity to irrelevant demographic cues and to prompt formatting shows the same 'salience-over-instruction' pattern; this paper is narrower (country-metadata + Brier loss on survey forecasts) but adds a paired-attenuation design that most prior audits lack.
entries.verify_note: Numbers and confidence intervals lifted verbatim; the 'ignore-disclosure fails' conclusion is directly stated in the abstract.

entries.title: Birfy/agentdescent
entries.author: Birfy
entries.summary: AgentDescent maps deep-learning training onto agent self-evolution: the 'parameters' are evolvable artifacts (skills, prompts, harness modules, verifiers), the 'gradients' are diffs with evidence cards, and the 'optimizer step' is a merge decision. N workers propose diffs in parallel and a barrier-free asynchronous aggregator resolves conflicts via a staleness filter, fusion tournament, and Beta-posterior acceptance. Governance is by blast radius: L2 skills merge freely, L1 harnesses/verifiers pass through an oracle, L0 safety/permissions are frozen.
entries.takeaway: The right abstraction for self-improving agent systems is not 'run and reflect' but a discrete-space optimizer over diffs with explicit conflict resolution, staleness policies, and blast-radius-gated merges. Freezing safety/permissions at L0 is the load-bearing safety property.

lessons.point: Diffs are not gradients: aggregation must be conflict resolution plus statistical acceptance plus transactional commit, not averaging.
lessons.excerpt: The one place the analogy *must* break defines the whole system: **gradients add, diffs do not.** Aggregation is therefore not averaging but **conflict resolution + statistical acceptance + transactional commit**.

lessons.point: Blast-radius tiers gate what may self-modify: L2 skills merge freely, L1 harness/verifier merges pass through an oracle, L0 safety/permissions are frozen.
lessons.excerpt: **Governed by blast radius.** Skills (L2) merge freely; harnesses/verifiers (L1) are forced through an oracle; safety/permissions (L0) are frozen.

lessons.point: For self-editing agent code, materialise the candidate in a throwaway workspace and overlay a pristine, frozen test suite after materialisation so the candidate cannot rewrite its own tests.
lessons.excerpt: `evolve_agent_code`, where the tree is **executed** behind a frozen test suite that the candidate cannot rewrite (pristine files are overlaid after materialisation, so weakening the tests at run time does not work either).

lessons.point: Parallel + async agent optimization beats a sync barrier by ~2.6-2.9x under heavy-tailed rollout latency (measured), because the round barrier waits on the slowest worker.
lessons.excerpt: the async pipeline is **~2.6–2.9× faster than a sync barrier** under heavy-tailed rollout latency.

actionable.title: Blast-radius-gated self-modification for agent harnesses
actionable.detail: Adopt AgentDescent's L0/L1/L2 framing whenever an agent is allowed to edit its own configuration: freeze safety and permission code at L0 (never mutable), force L1 (harness, verifier) changes through an oracle test suite that the candidate cannot rewrite (overlay pristine tests after materialisation), and let L2 (skills, prompts) merge freely. Pair with the frozen-test overlay pattern to prevent the candidate from cheating by weakening its own checks.

entries.prior_art: ADAS (Meta Agent Search), DGM (Darwin-Godel Machine), OpenEvolve, GEPA, EvoSkill — AgentDescent explicitly ports these as examples. The specific contribution is the async aggregator + blast-radius + frozen-test-overlay combination, which is a real delta over any single one of those.
entries.verify_note: All excerpts verified verbatim from raw file. Novelty scored at mid-range: the framing (diffs ≠ gradients) and frozen-test-overlay are genuinely new engineering ideas; the underlying self-evolution algorithms are ported from named prior work.

entries.title: PDF-to-markdown pipelines are the hidden token chewer inside enterprise AI adoption
entries.summary: Simon Willison surfaces leaked Accenture meeting audio in which the firm's agentic AI strategy lead identifies non-engineer users converting PDFs into images and then into markdown as a leading driver of internal LLM token spend. The takeaway is that document preprocessing choices, not model calls per se, dominate cost at scale.
entries.takeaway: Cost budgets die by a thousand PDF-to-image-to-markdown conversions, not by the model call at the end.

lessons.point: In real enterprise deployments, non-engineer users converting PDFs through image-then-markdown pipelines can dominate LLM token consumption.
lessons.excerpt: "We're seeing from some of the data internally at least that it's actually not our engineers that are driving the token consumption. It's a lot of the non-engineers that are doing some of those behaviors"

lessons.point: PDF-to-markdown conversion is called out by name as one of the biggest token chewers inside a large consultancy's own AI spend.
lessons.excerpt: "I'm learning that's one of the big token chewers," Henderson says. "Turning PDFs into markdown: is that right?"

actionable.title: Instrument document-preprocessing pipelines as first-class cost centers
actionable.detail: Track token spend by pipeline stage (raw file -> images -> markdown -> model call), not just per model. If non-engineer users are shipping PDFs through image OCR to markdown before calling the model, that stage is likely the top line item; cache converted artifacts and prefer native text extraction where possible.

entries.prior_art: toon-cuts-input-tokens-vs-json (ai-research claim on input-token accounting) and general Simon Willison cost-of-tokens commentary.

entries.title: Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding
entries.summary: G-STEER treats personalization of a deep-research agent as a pre-pipeline query-refinement step rather than modifying the agent itself: an 'Intent Elicitation Graph' organizes framing factors (user goals, constraints, preferences, evaluation criteria) with dependencies, and a learned clarification policy decides at each step whether to retrieve from user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine. The authors report the strongest weighted target coverage and highest downstream report personalization across two evaluated deep research agents (DRAs) while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline. The design keeps the underlying research agent unchanged — personalization lives entirely in a specification-refinement layer.
entries.takeaway: Personalize a deep-research agent by refining the *specification* before it hits the agent, not by modifying the agent itself — and use a dependency graph over framing factors to decide when to ask the user vs consult memory vs stop.

lessons.point: User context can be injected at two layers — inside the deep-research pipeline or into the input specification — and refining the specification lets you personalize with an unchanged downstream agent.
lessons.excerpt: User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent.

lessons.point: The clarification decision resolves three coupled sub-decisions: which framing factors matter, whether current context supports them, and which of retrieve-memory / ask-user / stop-and-refine is the right next action.
lessons.excerpt: This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query.

lessons.point: Structuring framing factors as an 'Intent Elicitation Graph' with dependencies lets a policy be trained on trajectories that span diverse factor-dependency and evidence-availability conditions.
lessons.excerpt: G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions.

lessons.point: The reported gain is not just quality — it is also asking users ~3x fewer questions than the strong clarification baseline while achieving higher personalization.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

actionable.title: Split a deep-research agent into a refinement layer and an unchanged execution agent
actionable.detail: If you are building a deep-research assistant, put personalization/clarification logic into a query-refinement stage that outputs a specification, then hand that specification to a stateless research agent. The refinement stage decides between (retrieve-memory / ask-user / stop-and-refine) using a dependency graph over the framing factors it still needs to resolve — a cleaner separation of concerns than editing the research pipeline itself, and empirically fewer user questions.

entries.prior_art: Extends the clarification-agent line (CLAM, ClarQ, InterCode-Clarify) and specification-decomposition planners; the new lever is the explicit dependency graph over framing factors combined with a spec-refinement wrapper around an unchanged DRA.
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b053-1.txt. Abstract-only; no numeric evaluation-detail claims made beyond what the abstract states.

entries.title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
entries.summary: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework for end-to-end RL training of agents inside real inference harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw). A lightweight proxy serves the harness's model calls and records them as training data for a standard RL codebase (veRL); a Kubernetes orchestrator runs each rollout in its own container. OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 / 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench; OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Ablations on harness choice find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others and that RL improves self-verification and tool coverage but leaves error recovery weak.
entries.takeaway: The core architectural move is decoupling training from inference by intercepting the model call at the harness proxy layer. That lets an existing RL stack train against a stateful, multi-process harness it can't natively express. The ablations are the useful evidence: harness choice matters for trainability, and RL does not fix error recovery.

lessons.point: A proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as RL training data is enough to decouple training from inference, letting a standard RL codebase train an agent inside an otherwise-opaque harness.
lessons.excerpt: OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale.

lessons.point: Harness choice materially affects trainability, and RL improves specific reliability behaviors (self-verification, tool coverage, multi-step plan completion) but not error recovery.
lessons.excerpt: We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

actionable.title: Intercept model calls at the harness proxy layer to make agents trainable
actionable.detail: If a project wants to RL-train an agent that runs inside a real inference harness (Claude Code, Codex, custom), the pattern to steal is the proxy-plus-orchestrator split: a proxy serves the harness's model calls and logs them as training data; a container orchestrator isolates each rollout. This gets end-to-end training against a stateful, multi-process harness without rewriting the RL stack. Also useful signal for evaluating your own harness choice: some are much harder to train against than others.

entries.prior_art: AgentGym, SWE-Gym, and RAGEN train tool-using agents but assume simpler harness structures. OpenForgeRL's contribution is treating a full production harness (Claude Code-style) as the training substrate, plus concrete ablations on harness choice.
entries.verify_note: Both excerpts appear verbatim in data/_raw/mrscan-b012-2.txt. No related_claims asserted.

entries.title: When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents
entries.summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate reusable skills from execution traces, but past a critical pool size added skills degrade performance. The paper argues contamination is structurally irreversible — once a defective skill is used to distill later skills, post-hoc removal recovers only a small fraction. Proposes Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): three critics (structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, semantic consistency) plus marginal-gain subset selection, filtering each skill pre-admission. Reports 72% pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 with a ~5x smaller pool that transfers to four other backbones.
entries.takeaway: Skill admission in self-evolving agents must be pre-commit, not post-hoc. Once a defective skill enters the decision context, its descendants inherit the flaw and rollback does not recover most of the loss — echoes the memory-poisoning principle: gate what enters, don't argue it out later.

lessons.point: Contamination in self-evolving agent skill pools is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after later skills have been distilled from it does not erase inherited flawed reasoning.
lessons.excerpt: We further show the contamination is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after the fact cannot erase the flawed reasoning its descendants have already inherited, so post-hoc rollback recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance.

lessons.point: Skill admission therefore has to be a pre-commit control, motivating a verifier-as-gatekeeper with three heterogeneous critics plus marginal-gain subset selection to catch combinatorial contamination.
lessons.excerpt: This makes skill admission a pre-commit necessity rather than a post-hoc fix, and motivates Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): a progressive trust hierarchy whose three heterogeneous critics - structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency - filter each skill individually, coupled with a marginal-gain subset selection that removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills reach the runtime context.

lessons.point: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional skill accumulation peaks then degrades and post-hoc removal recovers little — the empirical signature of irreversibility — while VaG improves every round to 72% pass@1 with a ~5x smaller pool that transfers to four other backbones.
lessons.excerpt: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation rises to a peak and then degrades, giving back most of its gains as the pool keeps growing, and post-hoc removal of the culprit skills recovers only a small part of the drop - the empirical signature of irreversibility. In contrast, VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution.

actionable.title: Gate skills at admission, not by post-hoc rollback
actionable.detail: In agent systems that accumulate reusable skills or long-term memory artifacts from execution traces, put admission gates (structural validity + behavioral safety + semantic consistency) in front of the pool. Do not rely on post-hoc removal — descendants inherit flaws and rollback recovers only a small fraction of the loss.

prior_art: Self-evolving / experience-distillation agents (Voyager-style skill libraries).
agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface claim — same 'gate at entry, not post-hoc' principle applied to memory.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts confirmed verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b052-3.txt. cluster=B (agents and harnesses): fits 'long-running agents / memory hierarchy'. Related_claim agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface confirmed present in claims.json — the paper's pre-commit thesis parallels that claim's 'validate what is allowed to ENTER memory rather than trying to argue it out later'.

entries.title: Counterfactual Simulation Training for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
entries.summary: arXiv paper (COLM 2026) introduces Counterfactual Simulation Training (CST), which rewards CoTs that let a simulator predict the model's outputs on counterfactual inputs. In cue-based counterfactual settings CST improves monitor accuracy by 35 points on models up to 235B parameters; larger models don't get more faithful CoT by default but benefit more from CST, and rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is 5x more efficient than RL alone.
entries.takeaway: CoT faithfulness can be trained for by rewarding CoTs that enable counterfactual simulation, materially improving CoT monitors — but the effect does not transfer symmetrically (dissuading vs persuading cues) and larger-by-default is not more faithful-by-default.

lessons.point: CST substantially raises CoT-monitor accuracy on cue-based counterfactuals (35 points) and improves simulatability on generic counterfactuals (2 points) at model scales up to 235B.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments with models up to 235B parameters show that CST can substantially improve monitor accuracy on cue-based counterfactuals (by 35 accuracy points) as well as simulatability over generic counterfactuals (by 2 points).

lessons.point: Larger models are not out-of-the-box more CoT-faithful; the benefit from CST scales with size, so faithfulness is trainable rather than emergent.
lessons.excerpt: larger models do not show more faithful CoT out of the box, but they do benefit more from CST.

lessons.point: Faithfulness gains do not generalize from persuading cues to dissuading cues, limiting deployment as a universal monitor.
lessons.excerpt: faithfulness improvements do not generalize to dissuading cues (as opposed to persuading cues)

lessons.point: Rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is a 5x more efficient path to faithfulness than RL alone.
lessons.excerpt: rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is 5x more efficient than RL alone

actionable.title: Treat CoT monitors as trainable and asymmetric, not free
actionable.detail: If a CoT monitor is part of the safety stack, CST-style training is worth evaluating — but bake in the asymmetry: gains on persuading-cue counterfactuals do not carry to dissuading cues, so measure both. Also note faithfulness is not emergent with scale; do not assume a larger model is a more monitorable model.

entries.prior_art: Sits in the CoT-faithfulness / CoT-monitoring line (Turpin et al., Anthropic CoT-monitoring work, Lanham et al.); the delta is using counterfactual simulatability as the training reward rather than post-hoc faithfulness metrics.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b009-4.txt. Cluster H (guardrails/alignment) fits because CoT-monitoring is a safety instrument. Novelty kept mid because CoT-faithfulness work has a substantial prior line; contribution is the counterfactual-simulation reward and the size-vs-training asymmetry finding.

entries.title: Fzkuji/OpenProgram
entries.author: Fzkuji
entries.summary: OpenProgram advocates 'Agentic Programming': one decorator (@agentic_function) turns a Python function into an agent where the docstring is the system prompt, type annotations are the tool schema, runtime.exec() calls are retryable DAG nodes, and everything else is plain deterministic Python. Context is an addressable node on a flat DAG (fork, spawn, cross-branch messaging follow from that), and code gates enforce validation the model cannot talk past.
entries.takeaway: The load-bearing idea is 'a code gate can't be talked past' — when a model's answer fails validation, it is sent back to re-decide, so critical steps cannot be skipped by prompt injection or hallucination. This is a stronger primitive than 'add a validator to your output parser.'

lessons.point: A code gate that re-asks the model on validation failure is a stronger control than a passive validator: it structurally forbids skipping the check.
lessons.excerpt: **A code gate can't be talked past.** When the model's answer fails validation, it is sent back to re-decide

lessons.point: Encode the tool schema in the Python function's docstring + type annotations rather than a separate JSON schema, reducing drift between the model's view of a tool and the code that implements it.
lessons.excerpt: **docstring** = the prompt · **type annotations** = the tool schema · `choices=[...]` = a code gate that re-asks until the answer is valid.

lessons.point: Context should be modeled as addressable nodes on a flat DAG rather than per-agent buffers, so fork, spawn, and cross-session messaging reduce to 'point at a different node set.'
lessons.excerpt: Context is an **addressable node, not a per-agent buffer** — so every multi-agent move is just "point at a different node set":

lessons.point: Hot-loading self-authored agent functions via a file watcher lets an agent grow its own tools without a create()/fix() control plane.
lessons.excerpt: the agent edits its own `@agentic_function` files with ordinary file tools → a watcher hot-loads them → the new tool is live on the next turn. No `create()` / `fix()` machinery.

actionable.title: Route every 'critical step' through a code gate that re-asks on failure
actionable.detail: For any agent step where a wrong answer costs money or damages state (payment routing, permission checks, tool selection), wrap the LLM call so the code enforces the acceptable answer set (choices=[...] or a validator). On any parse or validation failure, the code re-asks the model with the failure reason as context, instead of falling through to a default branch. This structurally prevents the model from 'skipping' the check via prompt injection, a bad completion, or a JSON-mode drift.

entries.prior_art: DSPy (Signature / Predict), Marvin's @ai_fn, Instructor's function-call retries, LangChain's @tool decorator — the 'docstring = prompt, types = schema' pattern is convergent. The 'code gate re-asks' framing and the flat DAG context model are the mild deltas.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. The arXiv id in the readme (2606.15874) is future-dated relative to typical arXiv IDs; not a claim we're relying on. Scored on the design ideas, not on the paper's peer status.

entries.title: "LLM Agent Performance" Is Not a Single Evaluation Target
entries.summary: arXiv position paper (v3) argues that a single 'LLM agent performance' number conflates three distinct evaluation targets: model comparison under a reference stack, complete-system comparison, and robustness across predeclared operating conditions. The claim a score supports depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy; the paper derives implications for leaderboards, reporting, and benchmark versioning.
entries.takeaway: Agent benchmark scores are only interpretable relative to a declared candidate boundary (model vs. full system) and condition policy (robustness scope); collapsing all three into one number is a reporting bug.

lessons.point: Agent benchmark scores are shaped not only by the model but also by harness, environment, evaluator, and inference budget.
lessons.excerpt: LLM agent benchmark scores are shaped not only by the model but also by the agent harness, environment, evaluator, and inference budget.

lessons.point: Model-comparison-under-a-reference-stack and complete-system-comparison answer different questions and should not share a leaderboard slot.
lessons.excerpt: Model comparisons under a reference stack and comparisons of complete agent systems answer different questions, while robustness asks whether either conclusion persists across predeclared conditions.

lessons.point: The claim a score justifies depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy, so reporting must expose both.
lessons.excerpt: The claim supported by a score therefore depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy.

lessons.point: Unified execution (same configuration across candidate models) is only one legitimate framing; robustness across predeclared conditions is a separate evaluation shape.
lessons.excerpt: Unified execution controls these non-model factors by evaluating candidate models under the same configuration, making observed differences more attributable to the models themselves.

actionable.title: Declare candidate boundary and condition policy alongside any agent benchmark score
actionable.detail: When reporting or consuming agent eval numbers, force a two-field disclosure: (a) candidate boundary — is this a model comparison under a fixed harness, or a full-system comparison? (b) condition policy — are results held under a single reference configuration or across predeclared perturbations (robustness)? Treat leaderboards that omit these as ambiguous.

entries.prior_art: Related to prior critiques of agent benchmarks (e.g., harness-sensitivity of SWE-Bench scores, contamination arguments, reproducibility studies). This paper reframes as a taxonomy of three distinct targets rather than proposing a new benchmark.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b009-3.txt. Position paper — moderate novelty and useful relevance to harness/agent-eval practitioners. Related claims chosen based on 'benchmark validity' theme without over-claiming refutation.

entries.title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
entries.summary: CASCADE is a biology-domain agentic framework exposing gene-perturbation prediction over MCP. The paper's biology-relevant portion validates predicted direction of change against real TCGA/METABRIC tumor data. The AI-relevant portion benchmarks whether an LLM agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP tool calls: across 35 queries, a local model reaches 71.4% exact match and a larger model 85.7%. Schema and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, and a targeted fix could not resolve this because the trigger condition never occurs.
entries.takeaway: Real-world MCP grounding on a scientific tool suite tops out around 71-86% exact match, and the residual failure is a confident wrong-perturbation-type call on ambiguous queries; scale reduces schema/alias mistakes but does not eliminate confident intent errors, and targeted fixes can be uninvokable because the ambiguity trigger never surfaces as an explicit signal.

lessons.point: LLM grounding of natural-language requests into a real MCP tool suite hits 71.4% (local) to 85.7% (larger model) exact match on 35 queries.
lessons.excerpt: Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model)

lessons.point: Schema and alias mistakes are fixable by scale or server-side correction, but confident wrong-perturbation-type calls on ambiguous queries are not.
lessons.excerpt: schema and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries

lessons.point: Targeted fixes for ambiguous-intent failures can be effectively uninvokable when the ambiguity trigger never surfaces at inference time.
lessons.excerpt: a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition never occurs

actionable.title: Measure MCP grounding as exact-match, and separate ambiguity failures from schema/alias failures
actionable.detail: When evaluating an MCP tool suite, report exact-match on natural-language-to-tool-call grounding separately for (a) schema/alias errors (which are largely fixed by server-side correction or larger models) and (b) confidently-wrong intent calls on ambiguous inputs, which are the residual failure class. Require an explicit ambiguity-check step or clarifying-question fallback rather than trusting a targeted patch that only fires when the model self-identifies uncertainty.

entries.prior_art: Extends prior agent-tool grounding evals into a real-domain MCP surface; consistent with 'agent tool selection can be steered by untrusted context' but the failure driver here is intrinsic ambiguity, not injection.
entries.threat: MCP tool grounding fails silently on ambiguous natural-language inputs by defaulting to the wrong operation with high confidence; downstream biological or clinical decisions could be based on the wrong perturbation type without any error signal at the MCP surface.
entries.conditions: Natural-language agent frontends to an MCP tool suite where multiple tool variants are semantically close (e.g., knockdown vs overexpression); no explicit ambiguity check or clarification step; residual ambiguity does not surface as a schema or alias mismatch.
entries.mitigations: Require the LLM to emit a confidence or ambiguity flag before invoking an MCP tool; add a clarification/confirmation step for tool variants that are semantically close; log per-tool exact-match grounding rates in production, not just tool-call success; separate schema and alias failure rates from intent-error rates when reporting.
entries.verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b048-3.txt. related_claims (agent-tool-selection-can-be-steered-by-untrusted-context, few-distinct-tools-beat-many) confirmed present in data/claims.json; not force-fitting a third.

entries.title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
entries.summary: Shadow-evaluation methodology: frontier agents are given the central open-ended research question of an unpublished paper (six days, thousands of dollars of compute), and the paper's original authors grade the output. Ran on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions. Agents completed all the engineering without human help but made no substantial research progress and were unambiguously rejected by both sets of authors. Five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the publishable-research bar, uncreative responses to design flaws, ineffective backtracking, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. Reproduced with a second model and scaffold.
entries.takeaway: The methodological contribution (author-graded shadow evaluations of unpublished work) is more durable than the point-in-time verdict. The findings themselves argue against strong 'AI does AI research end-to-end' claims: engineering is solved, research judgment is not, and the failures are consistent across scaffolds.

lessons.point: Agents can execute the engineering of an AI research project end-to-end but cannot substitute for the research judgment: two NeurIPS-quality open-ended questions, six days each, unambiguous rejection by the original authors.
lessons.excerpt: The agents completed all of the engineering without human help, yet could not make substantial progress towards answering the research questions. As a result, both papers were unambiguously rejected by the authors.

lessons.point: The failure modes are reproducible across scaffolds and cluster in taste/judgment territory, not compute: poor bar-setting, uncreative response to design flaws, weak backtracking, poor resource awareness, instruction drift.
lessons.excerpt: We identify five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the bar for publishable research, uncreative responses to shortcomings in the research design, ineffective backtracking from dead ends, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. A robustness check with a second model and scaffold reproduced these failures.

lessons.point: Shadow evaluation (author-graded, on unpublished work) is a cleaner probe than either narrow benchmarks or blind peer review of AI papers.
lessons.excerpt: Current evaluations either test agents on narrow, verifiable tasks, which excludes open-ended research, or submit AI-generated papers to blind peer review, which is overstretched, stochastic, and suffers from poor review quality.

actionable.title: Agent-driven R&D: engineering-complete, judgment-incomplete
actionable.detail: When evaluating agents for open-ended technical work (not just coding), separate 'can it execute' from 'can it decide what to execute'. This paper's five failure modes (bar-setting, creative recovery, backtracking, resource awareness, instruction drift) transfer cleanly to security-research agents doing exploit discovery or vulnerability hypothesis generation: the engineering runs will pass, the judgment will not. Design harnesses that route judgment calls to humans and let the agent execute the rest.

entries.prior_art: MLE-Bench, RE-Bench, and Sakana AI Scientist attempted narrow or peer-review-graded versions of the same question. Shadow evaluations on unpublished papers with author grading is the methodological novelty here.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in data/_raw/mrscan-b012-3.txt. No related_claims asserted.

entries.title: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
entries.summary: Longitudinal benchmark of 120 real-case-grounded finance tasks across 20 scenes and six domains, comparing four self-evolving agent scaffolds on Qwen3.7-Max with paired non-evolving controls. Reports Letta highest evolved score (91.65), Codex largest self-evolution gain (+19.37), and — most interesting for harness design — skill-only evolution beats memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution in Claude Code; rubric feedback beats reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds.
entries.takeaway: For self-evolving agents on professional workflows, three concrete design signals: (1) skill-only accumulation beats memory-only and combined skill+memory in the tested scaffold; (2) rubric feedback dominates reference-answer feedback across all scaffolds; (3) gains concentrate at harder within-scene ranks (4-6) — evolution helps most where the base agent struggles. Longitudinal design (paired controls, shuffled streams) is the reusable methodology.

lessons.point: Across four scaffolds, self-evolution improves score by 9.33-19.37 points and cuts compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task versus paired non-evolving controls — measurable transfer of experience across tasks in a professional workflow.
lessons.excerpt: Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task.

lessons.point: In Claude Code, skill-only evolution outperforms both memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution on task quality and compliance — evidence that persisting distilled skills beats persisting raw episodic memory or both together.
lessons.excerpt: In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution.

lessons.point: Rubric feedback (structured criteria) yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds — a general signal about how self-evolving agents should receive supervision.
lessons.excerpt: Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback.

lessons.point: Self-evolution gains concentrate at within-scene ranks 4-6 (harder cases) rather than the easiest 1-3, by 6.10-8.70 points — evolution rescues the tail, not the head.
lessons.excerpt: Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points.

actionable.title: Prefer skill-only accumulation with rubric feedback over episodic memory
actionable.detail: In agent scaffolds that persist experience across tasks: (a) accumulate distilled skills rather than raw memory (or both), (b) supervise with rubric criteria rather than reference answers, (c) evaluate longitudinally against paired non-evolving controls on shuffled task streams — not per-task in isolation. FinEvo-Bench provides the methodology template.

prior_art: Voyager-style skill libraries; agent memory design literature (MemGPT, Letta); AgentBench and SWE-bench (single-task, not longitudinal); rubric-based LLM-as-judge evaluation.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b056-2.txt. cluster=B (agents and harnesses): fits 'long-running agents / memory hierarchy' and 'agent evals'. related_claims: agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface is tangentially related (skill-vs-memory persistence choice), noted but not a strong support/contest tie.

entries.title: In-Context Examples Suppress Scientific Knowledge Recall in LLMs
entries.summary: COLM 2026 paper showing that adding in-context examples to LLM prompts on latent-structure-recovery tasks (chemistry reaction constants, econ demand elasticities, etc.) systematically shifts the model away from applying pretrained scientific formulas toward empirical pattern fitting, even when those examples were generated by the very formula the model would have applied. Documented across 60 tasks in 5 domains, 6,000 trials, 4 models. Accuracy can go up, down, or stay flat, but the strategy shift is consistent.
entries.takeaway: Few-shot examples don't just 'reinforce' knowledge; they can displace it. On tasks where the pretrained closed-form answer is better than curve-fitting to the demos, few-shot prompting silently makes the model dumber while looking like a helpful nudge.

lessons.point: Adding in-context examples systematically shifts LLMs away from using pretrained domain knowledge toward empirical pattern-fitting, even when the examples were generated by the very formula the model would have applied.
lessons.excerpt: We show that adding in-context examples makes models rely less on pretrained domain knowledge, even when those examples are generated by the very same formula. Rather than reinforcing knowledge-driven derivation, examples shift computation toward empirical pattern fitting.

lessons.point: The strategy shift is consistent across domains but its accuracy consequence is not: the same shift can lower, preserve, or raise accuracy depending on which strategy it displaces.
lessons.excerpt: This displacement is consistent across domains, but its accuracy consequences depend on how the displaced strategy compares to the one that replaces it: the same shift can lower accuracy, leave it unchanged, or appear to improve it.

lessons.point: For practitioners, few-shot examples should be treated as a strategy switch, not a knowledge booster.
lessons.excerpt: For practitioners deploying LLMs on scientific tasks, the message is cautionary: in-context examples may displace, rather than reinforce, the knowledge they are intended to support.

actionable.title: Audit few-shot demos for strategy displacement, not just accuracy
actionable.detail: When adding few-shot examples to a prompt for a task the model can also solve by recalling a formula/rule, the demos may silently shift the model from rule-application to pattern-matching over the demos. Accuracy alone won't reveal this; probe by comparing zero-shot vs. few-shot on cases where the closed-form rule and pattern-fit diverge.

entries.prior_art: Extensive prior work on few-shot brittleness (order sensitivity, format sensitivity, majority-label bias). This paper's specific finding — that same-formula demos still displace knowledge-driven derivation — is a sharper mechanistic claim than the usual 'few-shot is fragile' result.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract text at data/_raw/mrscan-b010-4.txt. No related_claims asserted; note this could feed a future claim on few-shot demos as strategy switches.

entries.title: Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability
entries.summary: Analyzes when innovation-residual audits can localize a bad operation inside an autonomous data-analysis agent's trace. Shows the choice of scoring window is decisive - short windows produce one flag per mistake but blur inherited errors, long windows spread one mistake across many operations. Gives exchangeability-based false-flag control and proves an identifiability floor: below a certain error magnitude, no such audit can attribute the fault, and the floor is dominated by representation dimension rather than training-data volume.
entries.takeaway: For agent-op forensics, the auditor's scoring window and the representation dimension are the binding constraints, not how many past 'good' analyses you collected. A hundredfold data increase moves the detection floor by under two percent.

lessons.point: Score choice determines whether an error can be localized at all - short comparisons cannot distinguish an inherited error from the original.
lessons.excerpt: The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations.

lessons.point: There is a hard identifiability floor: errors below a threshold cannot be attributed and the floor scales with representation dimension, not with the number of collected sound analyses.
lessons.excerpt: This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

lessons.point: False-flag control needs only that sound analyses be exchangeable, not that the fitted model be correct.
lessons.excerpt: we then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct

actionable.title: Log full operation traces for autonomous analysis agents so post-hoc audits can use variable window lengths
actionable.detail: If you plan to audit an agent's data-analysis trace after an incident, the auditor will need per-step context spanning multiple prior operations - not just the immediately preceding step. Store the full ordered operation log with inputs and intermediate outputs so window-length is an audit-time choice, and be honest that small errors cannot be attributed regardless of how much 'good' history you collect.

entries.prior_art: Innovation-residual and conformal-anomaly auditing exist in statistics; the contribution is applying them to agent traces with explicit false-flag control and an identifiability lower bound.
entries.threat: For a defender running an autonomous-analysis agent, small-magnitude adversarial or accidental errors sit below the audit's identifiability floor and cannot be attributed to a specific operation - useful signal for anyone assuming that 'more logged runs' will fix agent forensics.
entries.conditions: Applies to unsupervised-audit setups that learn from known-sound analyses and flag surprising operations; assumes exchangeability of sound analyses and controls only within-analysis false-flag rate.
entries.mitigations: Instrument agent runs with retained multi-step context; pick score-window lengths deliberately per-audit; treat below-floor errors as unattributable rather than absent; do not rely on collecting more sound analyses as a substitute for a smaller representation dimension.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts verbatim from the arXiv abstract at 2608.05490. Cluster J (observability, IR, forensics) fits: this is directly about post-hoc attribution of operations inside an autonomous agent.

entries.title: Zero Gap Is Not Restoration: Stratified Per-Question Probability Evaluation and Step-wise Mitigation of Benchmark Contamination
entries.summary: The paper argues that the dominant contamination-mitigation metric G-AP (Gap of Aggregate Performance) is misleading: discrete correct/incorrect readouts miss per-question effects, averaging before differencing lets over- and under-suppression cancel, and uniform per-question weighting can be gamed toward the clean model's high-frequency values. The authors propose SA-PPG (Stratified Aggregate of Per-question Probability Gaps), which samples per-question solve probabilities, differences against a clean model, and aggregates within clean-solve-probability strata. They also propose RailCap, a step-wise mitigation that caps trajectory tokens to the runner-up whenever a sample falls onto the greedy path, accumulating suppression until the distribution disperses. Under SA-PPG, prior mitigations' restoration is substantially overestimated and RailCap achieves the lowest gap.
entries.takeaway: Zero G-AP is not proof a contaminated model has been restored. Evaluate mitigation with per-question probability gaps stratified by clean-model solve probability; averaged aggregate metrics conceal over- and under-suppression that cancel. This is directly relevant to cluster-L integrity of eval sets against contamination, even though the paper does not frame itself as red-team methodology.

lessons.point: G-AP hides errors: discrete readouts and pre-difference averaging let over- and under-suppression cancel; uniform per-question weighting can be gamed.
lessons.excerpt: Discrete correct/incorrect readouts cannot characterize per-question performance, averaging before differencing lets over- and under-suppression cancel out, and uniform per-question weighting invites strategies to push solve probabilities onto the clean model's high-frequency values.

lessons.point: SA-PPG replaces discrete readouts with per-question sampled solve probabilities, differences per question, then stratifies aggregation by the clean model's solve probability.
lessons.excerpt: We propose \textbf{SA-PPG} (\textbf{S}tratified \textbf{A}ggregate of \textbf{P}er-question \textbf{P}robability \textbf{G}aps): estimate each question's solve probability by sampling, difference it against the clean model per question, and aggregate within groups defined by the clean model's solve probability.

lessons.point: RailCap sidesteps the estimate-then-suppress pipeline by judging contamination during generation: when a sample falls onto the greedy trajectory, cap the next token to the runner-up until the distribution is sufficiently dispersed.
lessons.excerpt: \textbf{RailCap} instead judges contamination during generation: whenever a sample falls back onto the greedy trajectory, the next trajectory token is capped to the runner-up, accumulating suppression until the response distribution becomes sufficiently dispersed.

lessons.point: Under the stronger metric, prior mitigations' claimed restoration is substantially overestimated.
lessons.excerpt: Across multiple contaminated models and benchmarks, SA-PPG reveals that prior strategies' restoration is substantially overestimated, while RailCap attains the lowest SA-PPG.

actionable.title: Don't trust averaged-gap metrics for contamination mitigation on your evals
actionable.detail: When claiming a leaked benchmark has been 'restored' by decoding-time mitigations, check per-question probability gaps stratified by a clean model's solve probability, not just the average performance gap. This applies to security-eval sets that may have leaked into pretraining — a zero average gap can hide cancelling over- and under-suppression.

entries.prior_art: G-AP metric and prior contamination-mitigation decoding strategies (estimate-then-suppress) are the direct baselines this paper contests.
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b007-3.txt line 10 (LaTeX \textbf{} markup preserved). Cluster L chosen because interests.yaml cluster L scope includes 'Red-team eval sets that don't leak into training data' — benchmark contamination measurement is directly the same integrity concern, even though this paper is not framed as red-team methodology. related_claims empty: no existing claim in claims.json addresses benchmark contamination evaluation metrics.

entries.title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
entries.summary: A benchmark and trace-logging framework for LLM agents that control microscopes. Across 105 agent configurations (1, 2, and 3-agent graph topologies, 5 LLMs, RAG and context parameters), 1,949 test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals, direct comparisons revealed clear latency, cost, and failure-mode differences, but surrogate models trained on architecture and test results did not reliably predict performance on new, unseen tasks. The heterogeneous test suite is useful for qualification, regression testing, and diagnosis, not for producing a task-independent global configuration model.
entries.takeaway: Benchmarks over agent architectures generalize poorly: even with ~2,000 runs and ~50,000 RAG retrievals across 105 configurations, surrogate models could not predict performance on unseen microscopy tasks. Agent-config benchmarks are useful for qualification and regression, not for picking a globally optimal architecture. This mirrors the SWE-bench generalization limitation at the agent-architecture level.

lessons.point: Surrogate performance models trained on agent architecture and past test results do not reliably predict performance on unseen tasks.
lessons.excerpt: surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks

lessons.point: Agent-architecture benchmarks are qualification and regression tools, not a search space for a task-independent optimal configuration.
lessons.excerpt: these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model

lessons.point: Even with 105 configurations, ~2K runs, and ~49K retrievals, the resulting corpus was insufficient to induce a global generalization model.
lessons.excerpt: In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded.

actionable.title: Treat agent-architecture benchmarks as qualification, not selection
actionable.detail: When picking an agent topology or LLM/RAG configuration, use benchmark results for regression testing and elimination of clearly-broken configurations. Do not extrapolate a globally 'best' configuration from bench results to unseen production tasks; require task-representative evals for each new deployment target.

entries.prior_art: Consistent with the broader 'benchmarks don't transfer' finding (SWE-bench generalization limits, capability elicitation gap); specializes the observation to agent-architecture selection for physical-instrument control.
entries.threat: Over-relying on a benchmark leaderboard to pick a production agent topology, LLM, or RAG configuration risks selecting a config that scores well on the qualification suite but fails on unseen production tasks.
entries.conditions: Selecting agent architecture from bench scores alone; benchmark test suite is heterogeneous but not representative of production task distribution; no task-representative evaluation before deployment.
entries.mitigations: Use benchmarks for regression and disqualification only; build task-representative evals per deployment; retain trace-logging of tool calls, RAG hits, and failure modes so the corpus can be inspected per task rather than aggregated into a single score.
entries.verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b048-2.txt. related_claims (swe-bench-doesnt-generalize-to-production-tasks, score-evals-on-groundedness-not-headline-f1) confirmed present in data/claims.json.

entries.title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
entries.summary: The paper proposes a six-level capability ladder for Economic World Models (EWMs), where heterogeneous agents (increasingly LLM-based) act, interact, and co-evolve with markets and institutions. A literature survey shows most work concentrates at the lower ladder levels; self-evolving agents and empirically-aligned economic twins remain rare.
entries.takeaway: For agent builders, EWMs are being pitched as high-fidelity multi-agent sandboxes for training, planning, evaluation, and safety — but the field is still parked at rule-based simulators, not adaptive LLM economies.

lessons.point: Economic World Models are framed as safety-relevant substrates: sandboxes where AI agents can be trained, planned, evaluated, and safety-tested against markets and institutions.
lessons.excerpt: high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents

lessons.point: A six-level capability ladder organizes agent-world systems, but existing work is concentrated at the bottom (rule-based / static-LLM agents) rather than at self-evolving agents or sim-to-real economic twins.
lessons.excerpt: existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare

actionable.title: Track EWM sandboxes as a candidate agent-evaluation substrate
actionable.detail: If you build agents, watch the EWM literature (see the authors' curated list at github.com/FreedomIntelligence/Awesome-Economic-World-Models) as a potential source of high-fidelity multi-agent test beds — but do not treat today's rule-based simulators as production eval harnesses.

entries.prior_art: Traditional agent-based economic simulation (Axtell, Farmer) and the Awesome-* curated list format. LLM-based multi-agent simulations (Generative Agents, Park 2023) already explored self-evolving societies.
entries.verify_note: Abstract explicitly supports the six-level ladder and the safety-substrate framing; no fabricated claims.

entries.title: VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation
entries.summary: The paper reports that off-the-shelf VLMs struggle to answer basic questions about racing video-game frame sequences (and the authors observe similar failures across other game genres), and studies concrete harness knobs — input sequence length, resolution, question batching — that affect both annotation quality and token consumption. Countermeasures raised include VLM output mixing (ensemble-style aggregation) and prompt optimization. The framing is practical: how to use a VLM as an annotator for reward-signal labelling in offline RL and conditioned training when the underlying scenes violate real-world physics assumptions.
entries.takeaway: VLMs used as annotators fail on synthetic (game) scenes even for basic questions; the practitioner levers that materially move quality vs cost are frame-sequence length, image resolution, and how many questions you batch per prompt.

lessons.point: VLMs adopted for video-game annotation face a domain-shift problem: synthetic scenarios are extremely variable and don't obey real-world physics, so out-of-the-box VLM competence transfers poorly.
lessons.excerpt: Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics.

lessons.point: VLMs fail on basic questions about racing-game frames — and the failure generalizes across other game genres — so you cannot assume a strong general-purpose VLM will annotate synthetic domains reliably.
lessons.excerpt: We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization.

lessons.point: Input sequence length, image resolution, and question batching are the concrete knobs that trade off annotation quality against token consumption in a VLM annotator harness.
lessons.excerpt: We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

actionable.title: Sweep sequence-length, resolution, and question-batching before scaling a VLM annotator
actionable.detail: When you plug a VLM into an annotation pipeline, do not commit to defaults. Run a small sweep across (frames-per-request, image resolution, questions-per-prompt) and measure both quality and token cost — the paper's finding is that all three axes materially move both quantities. Layer in output-mixing (multiple VLM answers merged) and prompt optimization for the residual gap before considering a fine-tune.

entries.prior_art: Fits the broader 'VLM-as-annotator / VLM-as-judge' literature (e.g., LLaVA-based annotation, GPT-4V labelling studies); the specific angle here is synthetic-scene domain shift and quantifying the length/resolution/batching trade-off, not the ensemble or prompt-optimization ideas themselves.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b053-4.txt. Cluster C (Model I/O and tokens) chosen because the concrete harness insight is a quality-vs-token-cost trade-off; the domain (video-game annotation) is adjacent, but the transferable lesson is about I/O sizing knobs.

entries.title: aeonfun/aeon
entries.author: aeonfun
entries.summary: Aeon is a self-hosted framework that runs agent 'skills' (markdown SKILL.md files with frontmatter + a prompt) on cron via GitHub Actions, across six harnesses (Claude Code, Grok, Codex, Pi, Vibe, Kimi). It leans hard on the 'no approval loop' pitch: read-only skills are quarantined from the repo, irreversible actions fail closed, and a Haiku scorer rates every run so a heartbeat/skill-health/skill-repair/self-improve loop can fix broken skills unattended.
entries.takeaway: The interesting bit isn't the marketing ('most autonomous') but the health loop: rate every run 1-5 with a small model, then auto-route low-scorers to a repair skill. Independent scorer plus capability tiers is a cheap self-healing pattern worth stealing.

lessons.point: A skill can be a single markdown file with frontmatter plus a prompt, portable across multiple agent CLIs behind one contract.
lessons.excerpt: A skill is a Markdown file: some frontmatter, then a prompt.

lessons.point: Autonomy needs capability tiers as brakes: read-only skills that can't write, irreversible actions that fail closed, and an optional per-run gate.
lessons.excerpt: Read-only skills can't touch the repo, irreversible actions fail closed, an optional [Fleet Watcher](../docs/CONFIGURATION.md#fleet-watcher-authorization-layer) gates every run, and secrets stay off the command line.

lessons.point: Self-healing agent loops can be built from a small-model per-run scorer plus dedicated health/repair skills.
lessons.excerpt: A model scores every run 1–5; `heartbeat` → `skill-health` → `skill-repair` → `self-improve` detect and fix broken skills without you

actionable.title: Add a per-run Haiku scorer + self-repair loop to any long-running agent
actionable.detail: For any unattended agent workflow, log every run's outputs and score them 1-5 with a cheap model on a fixed rubric. When the rolling score for a skill drops below a threshold, dispatch a repair pass that reads recent transcripts + the skill definition and proposes a fix PR. Combine with capability tiers (read-only / write / irreversible) so failed repairs can't do damage.

entries.prior_art: Voyager (Minecraft, Wang et al. 2023) demonstrated self-authored skills + a critic; AutoGPT's task queue; the specific 'markdown SKILL.md + cron + capability tiers' combination is a modest engineering delta over those.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. Marketing framing ('most autonomous') is unfalsifiable — scored on the concrete design bits, not the claims about 2M stars secured.

entries.title: universal-tool-calling-protocol/utcp-specification
entries.summary: UTCP is a specification for a protocol-agnostic tool-calling standard (HTTP, WebSocket, CLI, SSE, Text, and MCP) with a plugin architecture, expanded auth options, and comprehensive error typing. Positions itself as an alternative/complement to MCP.
entries.takeaway: UTCP treats MCP as one transport among many; for defenders, this means threat models built around 'MCP tools' need to generalize to any tool-calling transport, and tool-description injection remains a surface regardless of protocol.

lessons.point: UTCP aims to be transport-agnostic for tool discovery and invocation, spanning HTTP/WebSocket/CLI/Text/MCP.
lessons.excerpt: UTCP provides a standardized way for AI systems and other clients to discover and call tools from different providers, regardless of the underlying protocol used (HTTP, WebSocket, CLI, etc.).

lessons.point: v1.0 splits functionality into plugins per protocol, including an MCP plugin.
lessons.excerpt: Multiple Protocol Support: HTTP, CLI, WebSocket, Text, and MCP protocols via plugins

lessons.point: Enhanced auth (API key, OAuth, custom) is a core v1.0 addition, acknowledging auth as a first-class concern for tool-calling protocols.
lessons.excerpt: Advanced Authentication: Expanded authentication options including API key, OAuth, and custom auth

actionable.title: Generalize MCP threat models to protocol-agnostic tool calling
actionable.detail: When enumerating tool-poisoning and tool-description-injection risks, do not scope the analysis to MCP; UTCP-style abstractions push the same attack surface across HTTP/WS/CLI. Audit tool metadata handling in the caller regardless of transport.

prior_art: Model Context Protocol (Anthropic)
OpenAI function-calling / tool-use schemas
entries.threat: A UTCP-style abstraction over multiple transports widens the surface for tool-description injection and metadata drift: a poisoned tool description travels through the caller regardless of whether the underlying transport is MCP, HTTP, or CLI.
entries.conditions: Applies when an agent host adopts UTCP (or any transport-agnostic tool router) and trusts tool metadata pulled from third-party providers. Requires that the caller does not re-validate or sandbox tool descriptions on each fetch.
entries.mitigations: Treat tool descriptions from all transports as untrusted input, pin/checksum tool manifests, apply the same tool-description-injection checks used for MCP (see claim `mcp-tool-descriptions-are-a-prompt-injection-surface`), and use per-tool auth scoping rather than transport-level trust.

entries.title: Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI
entries.summary: Schema-based zero-shot extraction of hierarchical, variable-cardinality information from unstructured text in a single model call, paired with a path-based semantic-matching evaluator that classifies attribute matches as exact / semantic / useful / non-match using a generative comparator. Extracts 12 of 14 attributes at F1 > 90% on NICE HTA documents using Claude Opus 3, ~30x faster than a human domain expert, with reported cross-model and cross-organization transfer.
entries.takeaway: For hierarchical structured extraction, a single-call schema-driven prompt plus a path-based semantic matcher with a rubric (exact / semantic / useful / non-match) outperforms the usual exact-string-match evaluation and matches practitioner needs. The evaluator rubric is the reusable idea — most extraction pipelines still grade on exact string equality and undercount semantically correct answers.

lessons.point: Extraction of hierarchical, nested, variable-cardinality information runs in a single zero-shot model call under a schema — the schema itself encodes domain knowledge for both extraction and evaluation.
lessons.excerpt: The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.

lessons.point: A path-based semantic matcher aligns extracted-vs-gold attributes in nested variable-cardinality structures — this is the aligning primitive missing from most exact-match evaluators.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard.

lessons.point: The four-way match rubric — exact, semantic, useful, non-match — is domain-tunable and replaces binary exact-string equality with a graded verdict.
lessons.excerpt: We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.

lessons.point: On NICE HTA documents with Claude Opus 3, 12 of 14 attributes were extracted at F1 > 90% ~30x faster than a human domain expert, with reported cross-model and cross-organization/language transfer.
lessons.excerpt: We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of >90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was ∼30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert.

actionable.title: Use a path-based semantic matcher with a graded rubric for structured-extraction evals
actionable.detail: For extraction pipelines that produce nested/variable-cardinality output, evaluate with path-based alignment + a graded rubric (exact / semantic / useful / non-match) instead of exact-string equality. The rubric surfaces 'useful but not exact' matches that binary metrics wrongly discard, and captures the failure modes practitioners care about.

prior_art: Constrained-decoding and JSON-schema generation; LLM-as-judge evaluation for open-ended outputs; classic IE evaluation (MUC/ACE) using string-match F1; the constrained-decoding-for-structured-output claim in the ledger.
