entries.title: Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
entries.summary: Search2Skill argues that self-evolving skill libraries built purely from the model's own parametric knowledge or its past trajectories are capped at what the model already knows. It proposes a rubric-based RL loop that jointly learns when to search, how to search, and how to distill retrieved evidence into structured reusable skills, and reports gains from skill abstraction (not raw retrieved text) that transfer across model scales.
entries.takeaway: Self-generated agent skill libraries are bounded by the model's prior knowledge — closing capability gaps for expert domains means pulling in external evidence and distilling it, not just replaying good trajectories.

lessons.point: Skills built from a model's own parametric knowledge or its trajectories can't cross the model's knowledge boundary; expert-domain conventions have to be imported from outside.
lessons.excerpt: Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone.

lessons.point: A rubric-based RL objective can jointly optimize when to search, how to search, and how to write the resulting skill, rather than treating retrieval and skill-writing as separate stages.
lessons.excerpt: Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.

lessons.point: The gain does not come from stuffing retrieved text into the context — it comes from turning that evidence into an abstracted, reusable skill that transfers across model scales.
lessons.excerpt: Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

actionable.title: External-evidence step for self-evolving skill libraries
actionable.detail: In a harness that grows its own skill/prompt library from trajectories, add a capability-gap detector that triggers external retrieval, then a distillation step that abstracts retrieved evidence into a structured skill — copying raw retrieval into context is measurably weaker than the abstracted skill, per this paper.

entries.prior_art: Voyager-style self-evolving skill libraries; ReAct/Toolformer-style search-augmented agents; existing rubric-as-reward RL like OpenAI's RLAIF work.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b047-2.txt. Cluster B (agents & harnesses) fits since the contribution is a harness pattern for growing agent skills. Novelty is moderate — an incremental combination of known ideas rather than a new mechanism.

entries.title: EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents
entries.summary: EcoAgent-Bench introduces a 304-task benchmark where every task carries priced actions and an explicit budget, testing four decisions: avoid unnecessary escalation, escalate when local evidence is insufficient, select a model tier, and stop on unsupported premises. Micro-averaged accuracy is shown to reward one-sided policies, so the authors report an 'economic-consistency' score (worse of upgrade-oriented vs save-oriented family accuracy). Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% strict success and at most 7.3% economic consistency; a threshold-crossing budget sweep barely moves GPT-5.4's escalation rate (0% to 3%).
entries.takeaway: Completion-under-budget and economical action selection are distinct properties; a headline pass rate can hide always-escalate or always-cheap policies. Report the worse of upgrade-oriented and save-oriented performance.

lessons.point: Report the worse of upgrade-oriented and save-oriented accuracy, not the micro-average, to prevent one-sided policies from scoring well.
lessons.excerpt: Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure.

lessons.point: Tool-API agents score dramatically lower on strict economic consistency than on micro success (7.3% vs 24%).
lessons.excerpt: Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks.

lessons.point: Budget threshold sweeps barely change escalation behavior for a strong frontier model, suggesting escalation decisions are not straightforwardly budget-elastic.
lessons.excerpt: A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%.

actionable.title: Add economic-consistency scoring to agent evals
actionable.detail: When scoring agent harness runs that offer local vs escalated tools, split tasks into upgrade-oriented and save-oriented families and report the worse group score; a pass rate that averages both will mask always-escalate or always-cheap policies.

entries.prior_art: AgentBench, GAIA, HotpotQA / MuSiQue task families are re-used; the contribution is priced actions plus the split-family scoring.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts checked against fetched abstract verbatim.

entries.title: INTRYGUE: Induction-Aware Entropy Gating for Reliable RAG Uncertainty Estimation
entries.summary: The paper argues standard entropy-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) fails in RAG settings because induction heads that copy the correct grounded answer also trigger 'entropy neurons', inflating predictive entropy and producing false-uncertainty signals on accurate outputs. INTRYGUE gates predictive entropy on induction-head activation patterns and, across four RAG benchmarks and six open-source LLMs (4B-13B), matches or beats a wide range of UQ baselines.
entries.takeaway: For RAG systems, naive token-entropy hallucination detectors are miscalibrated in a predictable way: the same circuit that grounds the answer inflates entropy. Gating on induction-head activation partially separates the two signals.

lessons.point: Standard entropy-based UQ methods misfire in RAG because grounded copying and entropy-neuron activation are mechanistically coupled, so correct grounded answers can present as uncertain.
lessons.excerpt: while induction heads promote grounded responses by copying the correct answer, they collaterally trigger the previously established "entropy neurons". This interaction inflates predictive entropy, causing the model to signal false uncertainty on accurate outputs.

lessons.point: Combining a predictive-uncertainty signal with an interpretability signal (induction-head activation) yields a more reliable hallucination detector than either alone across 4 benchmarks and 6 open-source LLMs.
lessons.excerpt: Our findings demonstrate that hallucination detection in RAG benefits from combining predictive uncertainty with interpretable, internal signals of context utilization.

actionable.title: Don't trust entropy as a lone hallucination signal in RAG
actionable.detail: If a system uses token entropy as an abstain/route-to-human gate for RAG outputs, be aware it will false-positive on correctly grounded answers because of the induction/entropy-neuron interaction. Combining entropy with an internal 'was context actually used' signal is the direction of travel.

entries.prior_art: Semantic entropy (Farquhar 2024) and other UQ-for-LLMs work established entropy-family baselines. This paper's contribution is the mechanistic diagnosis of why they fail in RAG plus a gating fix; the mechanistic framing is the novel piece.
entries.verify_note: Both excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract text at data/_raw/mrscan-b010-1.txt. No related_claims asserted.

entries.title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
entries.summary: SearchAuditor introduces SearchAuditBench (1,243 failed deep-search agent trajectories averaging 73 messages and 65K tokens each) with expert annotations for critical error step, search-specific root cause, and reference repairs. Their multi-perspective auditor with evidence-grounded adjudication reaches 32.3% end-to-end pass rate versus 26.6% for the strongest baseline built on a frontier model.
entries.takeaway: Long-horizon search-agent trajectories are so noisy that even frontier-model auditors localize/repair failures under a third of the time — plan for auditor-in-the-loop, not one-shot triage.

lessons.point: Long deep-search trajectories are past human review scale, so failure diagnosis must itself be automated.
lessons.excerpt: Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity.

lessons.point: Even a frontier-model auditor tops out around 26.6% end-to-end on locating, attributing, and repairing search-agent failures — multi-perspective evidence-grounded adjudication only nudges it to 32.3%.
lessons.excerpt: even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%

lessons.point: Curated failure corpora (73-message, 65K-token trajectories with expert-annotated critical steps, root causes, and reference repairs) are the substrate for training and evaluating agent auditors.
lessons.excerpt: SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics.

actionable.title: Add auditor-pass over failed agent trajectories
actionable.detail: For any long-horizon agent harness, log full trajectories on failure and run a second LLM pass that must localize the first bad step, attribute a root-cause category, and propose a repair. Even with frontier models expect only ~30% end-to-end recovery — surface residual failures to humans rather than declaring auto-repair a solved problem.

entries.prior_art: General LLM-as-judge / trajectory critique work; adjacent to prior benchmarks like SWE-bench and AgentBench but focused specifically on failure attribution in deep-search trajectories.
entries.threat: Deep-search agents can produce fluent but wrong answers because small reasoning errors propagate through very long noisy trajectories, and the traces are too long for humans to audit.
entries.conditions: Multi-turn agent doing tool-heavy web search where each hop can compound reasoning error; failures surface only in the final answer with no per-step supervision.
entries.mitigations: Log full trajectories; run an evidence-grounded auditor pass to localize the first bad step and propose a repair; treat auditor pass-rate as a bounded assist (roughly a third of failures) and escalate the rest to human review.
entries.verify_note: All excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b047-0.txt. Novelty modest — failure-attribution benchmarks for agents are an active area; cluster J (observability/forensics for agents) is defensible.

entries.title: SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution
entries.summary: SkillTV-Bench is a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, targeting skill-aware trajectory verification (both LLM-as-Judge and Agent-as-Judge). The authors add SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable 'JudgeSkill' that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. An automated evolution loop over misjudged cases raises judge accuracy by 14.8 percentage points; in offline rollout-pool selection, trajectory-success rises from 22.9% at one rollout to 45.5% at ten.
entries.takeaway: Trajectory-level judging beats final-answer scoring for long-horizon agents, and encoding verification procedure as a reusable JudgeSkill measurably improves both accuracy and rollout selection.

lessons.point: Verification of skill-augmented agents needs procedural knowledge, not just the final answer, to decide what evidence to inspect.
lessons.excerpt: For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical.

lessons.point: Encoding verification as a reusable JudgeSkill and evolving it against misjudged cases yields a 14.8-point accuracy gain on the same judge model.
lessons.excerpt: On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points.

lessons.point: Agent-as-judge trajectory selection scales with rollout count: 22.9% -> 45.5% success from one to ten rollouts.
lessons.excerpt: In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts.

actionable.title: Evaluate agent runs on trajectory, not final answer
actionable.detail: When adding agent evals, log full tool-use trajectories and score them with a skill-guided judge that inspects intermediate artifacts, not only the final response. Final-response judges underweight task-critical failures in long-horizon runs.

entries.prior_art: LLM-as-Judge and Agent-as-Judge literature; distinguishes itself with directly inspectable artifacts and skills.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from fetched abstract.

entries.title: wanmol/goal-flow
entries.author: wanmol
entries.summary: goalflow is a LangGraph-based framework that transpiles Dify visual DSL exports into runnable, version-controllable Python and pairs them with a code-first agent SDK (agent_kit) — the sales pitch is combining visual workflow graphs with agent loops so a graph node can host an agent and an agent can call a sub-workflow as a tool. Its own README carries a public-warning: the .env* files were previously tracked and credentials still live in git history requiring git filter-repo and rotation before publishing.
entries.takeaway: The interesting artifact here is not the framework — it's the openly documented incident: even production teams shipping agent frameworks leak credentials into git history. Any 'we open-sourced our internal system' PR needs mandatory history scrubbing plus rotation as a gate, not an afterthought.

lessons.point: Extracting an internal agent framework into a public repo routinely leaks credentials via git history; scrubbing tracked .env files after the fact does not clean history.
lessons.excerpt: The `.env*` files are no longer tracked (a `.env.example` template ships in their place), but real credentials still live in **git history** — they must be scrubbed (`git filter-repo`) and rotated before the first public push.

lessons.point: Transpiling a visual-builder DSL (Dify) into runnable, version-controllable Python is a way to escape lock-in without losing the visual authoring surface.
lessons.excerpt: **Visual-first workflows** — design a flow in [Dify](https://dify.ai)'s drag-and-drop editor, then transpile the exported DSL into a runnable, version-controllable LangGraph Python file with one command. No lock-in to Dify's runtime.

lessons.point: For an I/O-bound async streaming pipeline, throughput scales with replicas rather than box size — measured 100 concurrent conversations on 2 vCPU / 4 GB per replica with no TTFT regression.
lessons.excerpt: a two-replica deployment on just **2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM per replica** sustained **100 concurrent conversations with no measurable regression in time-to-first-token**.

actionable.title: Gate every 'open-sourced internal agent framework' on a git-history secret scan and rotation
actionable.detail: Before an internal agent codebase goes public, mandate a two-step gate: (1) run git-history secret scan (gitleaks or trufflehog with --since-commit) across the full history, not just HEAD; (2) rotate every credential the scan finds, then use git filter-repo to remove the blobs. Simply untracking .env files leaves the secrets discoverable in older commits.

entries.prior_art: The Dify-to-code transpilation is convergent with efforts around n8n/Flowise exports; the git-history-secret hazard is well-known (see: signature-based-detection-fails-on-llm-authored-malware and related supply-chain claims). Notable here as an in-the-wild admission in the readme itself.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. Cluster is B (agent harness). The credential-leak lesson is the one item with independent value beyond the framework itself.

entries.title: Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay
entries.summary: Deterministic zero-model pipeline that compiles passive screen captures into typed activity frames (application, site, timing, input volume, evidence pointers). One-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 days shows 86x context reduction per day at 68 ms, with 98.4% agent QA accuracy vs 66-80% for LLM summaries.
entries.takeaway: A deterministic, byte-identical, model-free compiler over passively captured screen activity can shrink an agent's daily context ~86x while improving QA accuracy over LLM-summary baselines. Reported on a single-user corpus, so treat as prototype-level evidence.

lessons.point: A deterministic, model-free compilation of raw screen activity into typed frames yields byte-identical, cacheable, and auditable output — a property LLM summarization does not provide.
lessons.excerpt: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable

lessons.point: On the reported single-user corpus, compiled activity frames beat LLM summaries of the same capture at daily QA — 98.4% vs 66-80% — and a mid-tier model reading the block matches a frontier one.
lessons.excerpt: the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one.

actionable.title: Consider deterministic activity-frame memory for computer-use agents
actionable.detail: For computer-use agents that repeat routines, evaluate deterministic model-free compilation of screen activity into typed frames as a memory tier before paying frontier inference on every rollout. Note the reported evidence is a single-user corpus.

prior_art: Agent memory / long-running-agent compaction literature; computer-use agent papers.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts confirmed verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b052-1.txt. cluster=null: nearest cluster is A (retrieval and context) / B (agents), but the work is capability/cost focused with no security angle. Not tying to a claim to avoid forcing a fit.

entries.title: Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution
entries.summary: PMCoder is a repo-level LLM agent that pairs a hierarchical phase planner with an episodic memory, wired bidirectionally: the current plan phase conditions memory retrieval, and memory-derived trajectory statistics drive stuck detection and replanning. When issue-reproduction verdicts are available, they gate 'done' on execution evidence rather than the agent's own claims. On SWE-bench Verified the coupling adds ~5.0pp over a harness-matched baseline, with consistent direction across Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and an OpenHands port.
entries.takeaway: For long-horizon coding agents, treating planning and memory as coupled substrate (with an external execution-verified done-signal) reduces repeated failed edits, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion more than strengthening either alone.

lessons.point: Long agent runs fail because 'done' is inferred from the agent's own claims rather than from execution evidence.
lessons.excerpt: leaving long trajectories vulnerable to stale evidence, repeated failed edits, and verification inferred from the agent's own claims instead of execution evidence.

lessons.point: Coupling planning with episodic memory (plan conditions retrieval; memory stats trigger replanning) beats strengthening either alone.
lessons.excerpt: coupling planning and memory outperforms either component alone and reduces repeated failed actions, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion.

lessons.point: When available, reproduction verdicts should ground verification progress in execution evidence.
lessons.excerpt: When available, issue-reproduction verdicts ground verification progress in execution evidence rather than self-reported completion.

actionable.title: Require execution-evidence gates on coding-agent 'done' signals
actionable.detail: In any long-horizon coding-agent harness, do not let the agent's self-reported completion terminate the run. Wire a reproduction/test gate as the authoritative done-signal, and expose memory statistics (repeat-action count, empty-patch count) to a stuck-detector that triggers replanning.

entries.prior_art: Prior repo-level agents (Agentless, SWE-agent, OpenHands) strengthen planning or memory in isolation; PMCoder's contribution is the bidirectional coupling plus a reproduction-verdict done-signal.
entries.verify_note: All excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b002-0.txt abstract. Cluster B (agent harness design) is defensible; relevance to security engineer briefing is modest — this is agent-quality research, not agent-security research.

entries.title: Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention
entries.summary: Pulsar Attention replaces Star Attention's static prepended anchor block with a small attention-sink prefix plus Max-IDF-selected cross-block summaries, reducing Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3x on RULER with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at up to 128K tokens.
entries.takeaway: Content-aware summaries chosen by rare-token statistics beat content-blind anchors for distributed long-context attention, at identical KV-cache footprint.

lessons.point: Distributed blockwise attention methods have relied on a static content-blind anchor block, which this work identifies as wasteful.
lessons.excerpt: Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host.

lessons.point: Rare-token (Max-IDF) chunk selection plus a small attention-sink prefix can substitute for the static anchor while cutting compute.
lessons.excerpt: We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens.

lessons.point: The method claims up to 3.3x FLOP reduction over Star Attention while remaining competitive with dense attention up to 128K tokens.
lessons.excerpt: This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3x over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint.

actionable.title: Watch content-aware anchor replacements for distributed long-context
actionable.detail: If you run distributed long-context inference (Star Attention-style sharding), evaluate whether IDF-driven summary blocks give the same accuracy at meaningfully lower Phase 1 FLOPs before locking in a static anchor.

entries.prior_art: Star Attention (distributed blockwise attention) is explicitly the baseline; attention-sink tokens are a known softmax stabilization trick.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from raw fetched abstract. Cluster A (Retrieval and context) fits long-context/attention scope; but paper is purely performance-oriented, no security angle, hence low relevance.

entries.title: Every Cache Entry Earns Its Place: Global Allocation of Resolution and Coverage for KV Cache Compression
entries.summary: GraceKV frames KV-cache compression as global budget allocation over a prototype tree of layer-KV head-slot atomic units, adaptively trading coverage (adding tree roots) against resolution (splitting nodes) and holding up under 128x compression across long-context tasks without additional training.
entries.takeaway: Framing KV-cache compression as a global resource-allocation problem across layers, heads, and slots outperforms fixed-rule eviction or merging, especially at aggressive compression ratios.

lessons.point: Existing KV-cache compression methods use fixed rules that cannot flow resources across layers, heads, and slots.
lessons.excerpt: Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage.

lessons.point: A prototype-tree structure lets adding a new tree root expand coverage while splitting a node adds local resolution, both under one shared budget.
lessons.excerpt: Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache budget.

lessons.point: GraceKV holds up under 128-fold compression and ranks first in 24 of 32 experimental settings.
lessons.excerpt: Systematic experiments across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show that GraceKV ranks first in 24 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128-fold compression.

lessons.point: No additional training is required and inference stays on-GPU.
lessons.excerpt: GraceKV requires no additional training, and the entire compression and inference process is performed on the GPU.

actionable.title: Prefer global budget allocation for KV-cache compression
actionable.detail: If you deploy long-context inference and rely on fixed per-layer eviction or merging, benchmark against a global resource-allocation baseline before locking in the strategy; the reported robustness at 128x compression suggests headroom over fixed rules.

entries.prior_art: Token-eviction and token-merging KV-cache compression are the explicit baselines critiqued as fixed-rule.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Cluster A (Retrieval and context) covers long-context behavior and context compression, which fits KV-cache compression for LLMs. No security angle, so relevance stays modest.

entries.title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
entries.summary: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark of 22 task families (rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, volumetric deformable objects) with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables. It benchmarks Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families and evaluates 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by checking physical-law consistency and temporal stability of inferred parameters. Headline finding: no physics engine is uniformly faithful (largest gaps in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation), and video world models can generate motion with the correct equation form but wrong accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.
entries.takeaway: Generative video world models can fake the *shape* of a physical law while getting the underlying quantities wrong; perceptual-similarity evals miss this, so benchmarking has to compare inferred physical parameters against measured ground truth.

lessons.point: Existing physical-fidelity evaluations rely on perceptual similarity or human judgment, so they cannot say which physical principle a simulator or world model actually violates.
lessons.excerpt: existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated.

lessons.point: No single physics engine (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) is uniformly faithful; discrepancies concentrate in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation.
lessons.excerpt: Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation.

lessons.point: Video world models can output trajectories whose equation form looks right while the recovered accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing are wrong — a form-vs-quantity failure mode invisible to visual inspection.
lessons.excerpt: We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.

actionable.title: Evaluate generative simulators by parameter recovery, not perceptual similarity
actionable.detail: If you rely on a video world model as an implicit simulator, do not treat 'looks right' as evidence of physical fidelity. Fit the produced trajectories to the expected equations and check whether the recovered accelerations, momenta, and periods match ground truth. A model can nail the equation shape while getting the constants wrong.

entries.prior_art: Physics-engine benchmarking has been done piecewise (PhysGym, Kubric, PhysicsIQ); GAUGE's contribution is the joint numerical-simulator + video-world-model comparison with calibrated real-world trajectories and parameter-level diagnostics.

entries.title: SSTQ: Privacy-Preserving Vector Quantization via Subsampled Stochastic TurboQuant
entries.summary: SSTQ combines overcomplete equal-norm tight frames, coordinate subsampling, and privacy-aware 1D quantization for local-DP federated optimization; achieves optimal MSE scaling using only log2(N)+b bits per client with a codebook objective that cuts MSE from O(4^b) to O(2^b).
entries.takeaway: For local-DP distributed optimization, tight-frame quantization plus subsampling beats vqSGD-style geometric constructions on communication-utility trade-off.

lessons.point: Existing local-DP vector quantization (e.g., vqSGD) suffers unfavorable dimension-dependent variance.
lessons.excerpt: Existing vector quantization methods, such as vqSGD, use high-dimensional geometric constructions but incur unfavorable dimension-dependent variance.

lessons.point: SSTQ achieves optimal MSE scaling with only log2(N)+b bits per client.
lessons.excerpt: We show that SSTQ achieves optimal mean squared error scaling while using only ⌈log 2 N⌉+bbits per client, where N=Θ(d)is the frame size.

lessons.point: A surrogate codebook objective reduces codebook-dependent MSE scaling exponentially.
lessons.excerpt: We also derive a surrogate privacy-aware codebook objective that reduces the codebook-dependent MSE scaling from O(4 b)to O(2 b).

lessons.point: Analytical derivations were initially produced by an internal Gemini-based agentic system and human-verified.
lessons.excerpt: Some of the analytical derivations were first obtained using a fully automated Gemini-based agentic system developed internally at Google. The authors have verified those derivations and edited them for clarity of presentation.

actionable.title: Note LDP quantization advances for federated systems
actionable.detail: If you build federated learning with local differential privacy, benchmark SSTQ against vqSGD on the same task before assuming vqSGD-family quantizers are state of the art.

entries.prior_art: vqSGD is the named baseline. Local-DP mechanisms (randomized response, Laplace) are classical.

entries.title: openai/openai-agents-python
entries.author: openai
entries.summary: OpenAI Agents SDK is a provider-agnostic multi-agent framework built around a small set of primitives: Agents (LLM + instructions + tools + guardrails + handoffs), Handoffs (agents delegating to other agents), Guardrails (configurable input/output validation), Sessions (auto history), and Tracing. A SandboxAgent primitive runs agents inside a container for long-horizon file/patch/command work; UnixLocalSandboxClient runs it locally on macOS/Linux, DockerSandboxClient on Windows.
entries.takeaway: Modern agent SDKs converge on a small handful of primitives (agent, handoff, guardrail, session, tracing) plus a first-class sandbox client — sandbox-by-default is now table-stakes for long-horizon agent work.

lessons.point: Long-horizon agent frameworks expose sandboxing as a first-class primitive, not an afterthought.
lessons.excerpt: Use a `SandboxAgent` when the agent needs to inspect files, run commands, apply patches, or preserve workspace state across longer tasks.

lessons.point: Guardrails are surfaced as configurable input and output checks at the framework level.
lessons.excerpt: **Guardrails**: Configurable safety checks for input and output validation

lessons.point: Handoffs (agents-as-tools) are the SDK's recommended multi-agent primitive — one agent delegates to another via a tool interface rather than an ad-hoc router.
lessons.excerpt: **[Agents as tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/#agents-as-tools) / [Handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)**: Delegating to other agents for specific tasks

actionable.title: Treat sandbox-by-default as table stakes for any long-horizon agent
actionable.detail: When designing or auditing an agent harness, require that any agent doing file/command/patch work runs through a sandbox client (container, VM, or gVisor). The OpenAI SDK's split of SandboxAgent vs Agent is a useful contract to steal: separate the type so the runtime can enforce the isolation instead of trusting per-call flags.

entries.prior_art: LangChain/LangGraph agent primitives, CrewAI, AutoGen — the primitives here (agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing) are convergent industry patterns, not new; the SandboxAgent formalization is the only mild delta and even that mirrors OpenDevin/Devin-style workspace agents.

entries.title: CREBench: Evaluating Large Language Models in Cryptographic Binary Reverse Engineering
entries.summary: CREBench is a 432-challenge CTF-style benchmark built from 48 standard cryptographic algorithms and 3 insecure key-usage scenarios, with 3 difficulty levels and 4 sub-tasks from algorithm identification to flag recovery. Across eight frontier LLMs, the top model (called GPT-5.4) scores 64.03/100 and recovers the flag 59% of the time; human experts baseline at 92.19.
entries.takeaway: Frontier LLMs are meaningfully useful at cryptographic binary reverse engineering (~60% flag-recovery at the top) but still trail expert humans by a wide margin; treat LLM-only crypto-RE output as an accelerator that needs expert verification, not a replacement.

lessons.point: The best evaluated frontier LLM recovers the flag on 59% of cryptographic binary RE challenges in this benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: GPT-5.4, the best-performing model, achieves 64.03 out of 100 and recovers the flag in 59\% of challenges

lessons.point: Human experts still substantially outperform frontier LLMs on cryptographic reverse engineering.
lessons.excerpt: We also establish a strong human expert baseline of 92.19 points, showing that humans maintain an advantage in cryptographic RE tasks.

actionable.title: Use LLM crypto-RE as a triage layer, not an oracle
actionable.detail: For crypto-heavy binary analysis workflows, use frontier LLMs to shortlist algorithm identification and key-usage anti-patterns, then hand off to a human expert for flag/vuln confirmation. Do not accept an LLM-only crypto-RE result as a security finding.

entries.prior_art: Sits alongside other LLM-for-RE benchmarks (e.g. asm2source style, BinaryCorp variants); specializes to cryptographic algorithms and CTF-style flag recovery.

entries.title: Ask-E: An Environment for Calibrated Question Generation
entries.summary: Ask-E flips the eval loop: instead of training models to answer hard problems, it benchmarks and trains them to generate problems calibrated to a target skill level (exactly one of two reference models can solve it). Training on the generator objective transfers to downstream math benchmarks without new math data or stronger-model supervision. Marginal relevance to security evals — the calibration idea is transferable but no security-specific application here.
entries.takeaway: Generating calibrated questions is itself an eval signal; hard-to-generate problems require capability beyond the target — useful framing for keeping red-team/eval sets ahead of the model.

lessons.point: A generator that produces problems only one of two reference models can solve is a lower-bound witness that the generator has capability beyond the weaker model — inverts the usual answer-based eval.
lessons.excerpt: A generated question is successfully calibrated if exactly one of the two models can solve it, placing it precisely within the target range and differentiating the capabilities of these models.

lessons.point: Training on question generation transfers to answering — improved downstream math benchmarks without additional math training data, stronger-teacher interaction, or correctness reward.
lessons.excerpt: We also show that training on this environment leads to improvements across a number of downstream math benchmarks even with no new math data, no interaction with stronger models, and no correctness-based reward.

lessons.point: Frontier models remain far from saturating calibrated generation, so it works as a live benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: We find that even frontier models achieve below 50% calibration on the benchmark, leaving significant headroom to measure future progress.

actionable.title: Consider inverted-eval framing for red-team set generation
actionable.detail: For red-team/jailbreak eval sets that need to stay ahead of the model, consider a generator target that produces prompts exactly one of two candidate models trip on — treats calibration itself as the eval signal. Note: paper is math-only; no security transfer demonstrated.

entries.prior_art: Adversarial/synthetic problem generation for eval (WildBench-style pairwise difficulty, self-play question generation, evolving jailbreak suites like PAIR/TAP). Calibration-via-two-model-bracket framing is a modest refinement, not a new category.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in raw text. Related claims cited as adjacent context (eval design, dataset-leakage risk); paper does not directly support/refute them. cluster=null — adjacent, no direct security claim work.

entries.title: Beyond Scaffold Splits: Structural-Frontier Evaluation Reveals Hidden Failures in ADMET Models
entries.summary: Argues that Bemis-Murcko scaffold holdouts underestimate ADMET-model error on truly novel chemistry. Introduces a label-free structural-frontier split that reserves the sparsest, most physicochemically remote scaffolds and shows large error inflation (taskwise median 87.0%, mean 130.3%) versus a matched scaffold control. Tested robust-training penalties (MV-FREX and three others) do not close the gap.
entries.takeaway: OOD splits chosen by convention can hide model failure at the true generalization frontier; the same critique likely applies to LLM benchmarks, though the paper is chemistry-specific.

lessons.point: The choice of holdout split, not just model capacity, determines whether OOD failure is visible; a frontier-based split inflates error dramatically over the standard scaffold split.
lessons.excerpt: Against a 70/10/20 scaffold control with identical acyclic grouping, the frontier inflates equally weighted primary error with a taskwise median of 87.0% and a skew-sensitive mean of 130.3%

lessons.point: A graph-network head still shows a large frontier gap, so the effect is not explained by low model capacity.
lessons.excerpt: A message-passing graph-network control still shows a large gap (mean 82.8% over four tasks) and does not invert, so a low-capacity head does not explain the effect.

lessons.point: Tested tail-risk and robust-loss penalties fail to reduce frontier error, so split construction and label provenance are load-bearing evaluation constraints in their own right.
lessons.excerpt: Split construction and label provenance are important evaluation constraints in their own right, and the tested training penalties do not resolve the frontier failures we observe.

actionable.title: Analog for LLM eval design: pick holdouts that stress the true frontier
actionable.detail: When building or reviewing eval sets, avoid identifiers-of-convenience (scaffolds, source-domain tags, dataset splits inherited from prior work). Construct a label-free 'frontier' split that reserves the most dissimilar inputs and report both. The finding that a training-time robust penalty does not close the gap generalizes: eval-set curation dominates model-side patches.

entries.prior_art: Standard Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits and the more recent Lo-Hi and DataSAIL splitters, against which this frontier split is compared and shown to be harder on average.

entries.title: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders: Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks on Symmetric Data
entries.summary: Extends the Linear Representation Hypothesis behind sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to account for data symmetries. Shows on synthetic and scientific datasets that equivariant SAEs avoid failure modes of ordinary SAEs on symmetric data and can produce more useful downstream features despite worse reconstruction, arguing reconstruction is a poor proxy for interpretability.
entries.takeaway: Reconstruction quality can be inversely correlated with feature usefulness for SAEs under symmetries, which weakens reconstruction-based interpretability benchmarks even though the paper focuses on scientific rather than safety-relevant models.

lessons.point: SAE unidentifiability worsens on symmetric data, and priors like equivariance are needed for stable interpretations.
lessons.excerpt: We show that this problem is exacerbated by data symmetries such as rotations that are prevalent in scientific domains.

lessons.point: Reconstruction quality is not a reliable proxy for how useful SAE features are downstream.
lessons.excerpt: reconstruction quality can be inversely correlated with feature usefulness under symmetries, cautioning against its use as a key measure of interpretability

lessons.point: Equivariant SAEs can find features that improve downstream tasks even when their reconstruction gets worse.
lessons.excerpt: the resulting Equivariant SAEs can (1) avoid the pitfalls of existing SAEs on symmetric data and (2) discover features more useful for downstream tasks despite worse reconstructions

actionable.title: Flag caveat: reconstruction is a weak SAE metric
actionable.detail: If any downstream security-adjacent work leans on SAE reconstruction to justify interpretability claims (e.g., steering / refusal-direction work), note this paper as a specific reason to require task-side utility metrics alongside reconstruction.

entries.prior_art: Linear Representation Hypothesis, Anthropic/DeepMind SAE and dictionary-learning interpretability, group-equivariant CNNs (Cohen & Welling).
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from the arxiv abstract; scientific-data framing keeps this well outside AI-security scope, so cluster=null and low relevance.

entries.title: Multi-Level Modeling of Large Language Model Inference Latency and Energy via Hybrid Analytical--Machine-Learning Predictors
entries.summary: HYMELL is a three-level predictor for LLM inference latency and energy that combines analytical modeling of primitive operations, ML prediction of higher-level components, and an end-to-end model for system overheads across prefill and decode. It covers dense and MoE FFNs and MHA/GQA attention, and reports under 5% error on LLaMA 3 8B on an NVIDIA H100. The pitch is fast, hardware-free design-space exploration for latency/energy-aware LLM deployment.
entries.takeaway: Cost/latency estimation for LLM inference is being reframed as a hardware-free predictor problem, decoupled from actually running the model. For deployment decisions this is useful, but the reported accuracy is a single-GPU, single-model figure — treat it as evidence the approach works on one H100 + LLaMA 3 8B rather than a general-purpose estimator.

lessons.point: Splitting the estimator into analytical primitives + ML for higher-level components + an end-to-end system model captures both prefill and decode phase overheads that pure-analytical or pure-ML predictors miss.
lessons.excerpt: HYMELL models LLM execution through a three-level hierarchy: analytical estimation of primitive operations, ML prediction of higher-level components, and an end-to-end model that captures system-level overheads across both prefill and decode phases.

lessons.point: On a single hardware target the predictor reports high accuracy, which supports using it for design-space exploration without booting the model.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 graphics processing unit (GPU), HYMELL achieves high predictive accuracy; notably, for LLaMA 3 8B, it attains less than 5% error for both prefill and decode phases.

actionable.title: Use hardware-free LLM cost predictors for capacity/routing decisions, not for SLA guarantees
actionable.detail: When choosing between MoE vs dense, GQA vs MHA, or provisioning for a new context length, a predictor like HYMELL can rank options without booting hardware. Do not stake latency SLAs on <5% error extrapolated off one H100 + LLaMA 3 8B calibration — the paper's accuracy claim is bounded to that setup.

entries.prior_art: Analytical roofline models and ML-based predictors for GPU workloads exist; HYMELL is the hybrid variant specialized for LLM prefill+decode.

entries.title: Rethinking Evaluation Paradigms in IBP-based Certified Training
entries.summary: ICML 2026 paper arguing that certified-training methods for adversarial robustness should be evaluated on the Pareto front of natural vs certified accuracy rather than a single hyperparameter configuration. The authors run multi-objective HPO and find prior configurations were substantially undertuned, so reported gains between methods are smaller than assumed.
entries.takeaway: Single-config accuracy numbers over-state progress in certified-training research; Pareto-front comparisons after multi-objective tuning are the more honest bar. Relevant to red-teamers and evaluators building adversarial-robustness benchmarks that need to stay honest across method generations.

lessons.point: Reporting a single natural-vs-certified accuracy point misleads comparisons between certified-training methods, because the metrics are inherently conflicting.
lessons.excerpt: Because these metrics are inherently conflicting, the common practice of reporting a single configuration is problematic: it can mislead conclusions about overall performance and prevents unbiased assessments of the state of the art.

lessons.point: Automated multi-objective HPO reveals prior published configurations were substantially undertuned, so headline gains are smaller than assumed.
lessons.excerpt: This approach often uncovers substantial undertuning in previously reported configurations, yielding superior performance and establishing a new state of the art.

lessons.point: Multi-objective comparison exposes performance complementarities between certified-training methods that single-config reporting hides.
lessons.excerpt: Leveraging these fronts, we present the first comprehensive multi-objective comparison of certified training approaches, showing that prior advancements are less pronounced than assumed and revealing previously unreported performance complementarities.

actionable.title: Score robustness methods on Pareto fronts, not single configs
actionable.detail: When comparing certified-training methods (or any defense with a natural-vs-defended trade-off), publish Pareto-optimal configurations from multi-objective HPO rather than one point per method. Otherwise apparent progress is confounded with tuning budget.

entries.prior_art: Prior IBP/CROWN-IBP certified-training papers reported single natural/certified accuracy pairs; multi-objective evaluation of adversarial-training methods has been discussed but is not the norm.
entries.threat: Overstated adversarial robustness claims propagate into downstream defender product decisions when the defense literature reports cherry-picked hyperparameter configurations.
entries.conditions: Comparing two certified-training or adversarial-training methods using their originally-published hyperparameters, on the same architecture and threat model.
entries.mitigations: Run multi-objective hyperparameter optimisation for each method, publish the Pareto front over natural vs certified accuracy, and pick operating points by application-level risk tolerance rather than a single headline number.

entries.title: SAGEO Arena: A Realistic Environment for Evaluating Search-Augmented Generative Engine Optimization
entries.summary: KDD 2026 paper introducing SAGEO Arena, an end-to-end evaluation environment for Search-Augmented Generative Engine Optimization: the practice of optimizing web documents to raise their visibility in AI-generated answers. Existing benchmarks skip retrieval/reranking and strip structural markup; SAGEO Arena keeps both. Finds current SEO/GEO strategies often degrade performance under a realistic pipeline and that structural (schema) markup helps.
entries.takeaway: SAGEO is the SEO of the LLM era. Realistic end-to-end evaluation shows most optimization tricks that look good on toy benchmarks hurt real retrieval/reranking. Adjacent to prompt-injection-via-web-content but this paper is about visibility, not defense.

lessons.point: Benchmarks that pre-select candidate documents and strip schema markup systematically overestimate SAGEO strategy effectiveness.
lessons.excerpt: existing benchmarks lack end-to-end visibility evaluation of optimization strategies, operating on pre-determined candidate documents that abstract away retrieval and reranking preceding generation. Moreover, existing benchmarks discard structural information (e.g., schema markup) present in real web documents, overlooking the rich signals that search systems actively leverage in practice.

lessons.point: Under realistic conditions, current SAGEO tactics frequently degrade retrieval and reranking rather than improve them, and successful optimization must be tailored per pipeline stage.
lessons.excerpt: Our findings reveal that existing approaches remain largely impractical under realistic conditions and often degrade performance in retrieval and reranking. We also find that structural information helps mitigate these limitations, and that effective SAGEO requires tailoring optimization to each pipeline stage.

actionable.title: SAGEO Arena is a candidate testbed for indirect-prompt-injection experiments on real search pipelines
actionable.detail: The environment reproduces a full generative search pipeline over real web docs including schema markup, which is the exact surface exploited by indirect prompt injection. If Track B ever grows an experimental arm, this is a plausible harness to test injection payloads end-to-end without standing up a bespoke pipeline.

prior_art: Prior GEO/SEO-for-LLMs work (Aggarwal et al. 'GEO: Generative Engine Optimization', 2024); RAG evaluation harnesses like RAGGED, RGB; adversarial-web-document work on injecting instructions into scraped pages.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from arXiv abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b015-1.txt. Topic kept as ai-research; only mild adjacency to AI security (via indirect prompt injection over web corpora). Cluster left null because no existing cluster targets SEO-for-LLMs, and no claim in data/claims.json matches.

entries.title: SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation
entries.summary: Proposes SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework for autonomous, test-time evolution of LLM agent skills. Combines falsifiable hypothesis generation with evidence-guided tree search over skill-revision branches, addressing the sparse-reward trap where greedy refinement of a single incumbent skill wastes limited trials. Evaluated on 87 SkillsBench tasks; reports 55.9% (GPT-5.3-Codex) and 57.9% (Claude Opus 4.7) average pass rate under a five-iteration budget.
entries.takeaway: For agent skill self-evolution under tight interaction budgets, hypothesis-driven tree search over multiple candidate skills outperforms greedy single-branch refinement, because sparse-reward outcomes conflate multiple failure causes and mislead single-incumbent methods.

lessons.point: Sparse-reward agent skill refinement suffers an exploitation trap where early misdiagnoses burn the limited trial budget on unproductive trajectories.
lessons.excerpt: Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories.

lessons.point: Translating failure hypotheses into executable tests yields dense diagnostic reward without extra environment attempts, enabling more efficient search over skill revisions.
lessons.excerpt: SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts.

lessons.point: On SkillsBench, average pass rate reaches 55.9% with GPT-5.3-Codex and 57.9% with Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget.
lessons.excerpt: SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

actionable.title: Prefer branching self-verification over greedy skill refinement
actionable.detail: If you build a self-evolving agent skill system with a small trial budget, avoid single-incumbent greedy refinement; keep multiple skill-revision branches alive and use falsifiable in-code checks as a dense reward signal.

entries.prior_art: Self-refine, Reflexion, and tree-of-thought variants for agent skill evolution.

entries.title: Topology-Aware Data Movement for Disaggregated GPU Inference
entries.summary: A KV-cache transfer orchestrator for disaggregated prefill/decode inference that discovers interconnect hierarchy and picks NVLink/PCIe/IB/TCP per transfer, with pipelined layer-by-layer transfers and CXL 3.0 overflow tier; projected 3-18x latency reduction over uniform RDMA.
entries.takeaway: Uniform RDMA for KV-cache transfer wastes up to 72x bandwidth headroom; topology-aware transport selection and pipelining reclaim most of it.

lessons.point: Disaggregated inference forces per-request KV-cache transfers on the order of 1.3 GB (Llama-70B) reaching 100 GB/s at production scale.
lessons.excerpt: When prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, the KV cache must be transferred between them. For a 70B model this is 1.3 GB per request, exceeding 100 GB/s aggregate at production scale.

lessons.point: Existing production systems ignore that GPU-to-GPU bandwidth varies by up to 72x with physical topology.
lessons.excerpt: Yet DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake all use uniform RDMA, ignoring that bandwidth between two GPUs varies by 72x depending on their physical relationship: 900 GB/s via NVLink 4.0 within a domain (1.8 TB/s on NVLink 5, widening the gap to 144x), 50 GB/s via InfiniBand across nodes, 12.5 GB/s via TCP across data centers.

lessons.point: Pipelined layer-by-layer transfer overlapped with ongoing prefill hides 76-100% of transfer latency behind computation.
lessons.excerpt: pipelined layer-by-layer transfer that overlaps transmission with ongoing prefill, hiding 76 to 100 percent of transfer latency behind computation depending on transport, with NVLink and PCIe transfers hidden entirely

lessons.point: The authors explicitly cannot run a full evaluation because the hardware is beyond academic reach; results are projected.
lessons.excerpt: Full evaluation requires multi-node clusters with heterogeneous interconnects and CXL 3.0 hardware that is beyond academic resources and not yet available in GPU clouds.

actionable.title: Design KV-cache transport by topology, not uniformly
actionable.detail: If you run disaggregated prefill/decode on heterogeneous interconnects, pick transport per pair (NVLink domain, PCIe, IB, TCP) and pipeline layer-by-layer with prefill; uniform RDMA leaves substantial latency on the table.

entries.prior_art: DistServe, Splitwise, Mooncake are the named baselines. Attention-sink and CXL memory-tiering research exists separately.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Serving-infra paper with no security angle; cluster=null. Note the projected-not-measured caveat: authors admit they lack hardware to fully evaluate.

entries.title: Revisiting Black-Box Model Ownership Verification through Information Theory
entries.summary: Analyzes the robustness-utility trade-off in black-box model watermarking through an information-theoretic lens, identifies a capacity crisis when only predicted labels are used, and proposes a watermarking scheme that exploits the top-k output space instead. Evaluated across image, text, and tabular domains.
entries.takeaway: Label-only black-box watermarks lack enough channel capacity to encode robust ownership signals without hurting predictive accuracy; using top-k output opens more capacity for a better robustness-utility trade-off.

lessons.point: Frames the watermarking trade-off as an information-theoretic capacity problem rather than a heuristic tuning problem.
lessons.excerpt: we analyze this limitation from an information-theoretic perspective and identify a fundamental capacity crisis: relying solely on predicted labels provides insufficient capacity to embed robust ownership signals without degrading accuracy.

lessons.point: Proposes using the top-k output (not just argmax label) as the richer channel for the watermark.
lessons.excerpt: we propose a new black-box ownership verification framework that leverages the top-k output. By exploiting this richer output space, our approach increases the effective capacity available for watermarking while preserving predictive performance.

actionable.title: If you rely on watermarks for model ownership, expose top-k, not just labels
actionable.detail: Operationally minor for most agent-security work. But if you own a hosted classifier and use watermarking as an ownership signal, deploying top-k output access materially widens the watermark's effective channel; deploying label-only closes it.

entries.prior_art: Extends existing black-box watermarking literature that has repeatedly hit the robustness-vs-utility wall; the information-theoretic framing is the new contribution.

entries.title: Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry
entries.summary: Autonomy-of-Heads (AoH) is a data-free method that classifies attention heads as retrieval or streaming by the spectral geometry of their weight-space query-key projections, avoiding runtime attention scores or calibration prompts. Concentrated spectra flag retrieval heads; diffuse spectra flag streaming heads. At 50% sparsity the abstract reports retention of 96.5% of Full Attention performance on average, with up to 41.4% prefill and 66.0% decode latency reduction and 50.0% KV-cache memory reduction at 256K tokens.
entries.takeaway: Head function (retrieval vs streaming) can be diagnosed from static QK weight geometry rather than from runtime traffic, which removes the calibration-data dependency of prior sparse-attention schemes.

lessons.point: Prior sparse-attention head diagnosis is input-dependent and costly to deploy.
lessons.excerpt: Existing sparse attention and KV-compression methods typically decide which tokens or heads to preserve from runtime attention scores, observation windows, calibration prompts, or learned gates, making head diagnosis input-dependent and costly to deploy.

lessons.point: Retrieval vs streaming heads separate along the effective-rank of the query-key kernel.
lessons.excerpt: concentrated spectra indicate a small number of dominant query-key matching directions and are associated with retrieval heads, whereas diffuse spectra indicate the absence of a dominant global matching direction and are associated with streaming heads.

lessons.point: At 50% sparsity, AoH retains ~96.5% of Full Attention with substantial latency and KV-cache savings.

entries.title: Same Answer, Different Confidence: Protocol Sensitivity in LLM Confidence Calibration
entries.summary: Paper auditing how the choice of measurement protocol (which answer is scored, under which prompt, which readout) determines whether verbalized confidence or token-likelihood confidence appears better calibrated. Across four QA datasets and three 7-8B instruct models, the ranking flips in 4 of 12 settings under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC purely from protocol choice. In a twelve-study audit, five prior comparisons never state the protocol.
entries.takeaway: Whether verbalized confidence beats token-likelihood confidence is not a property of the model; it is a property of the (answer, context, readout) protocol, and published comparisons routinely leave that protocol unspecified.

lessons.point: Twelve operational-protocol variants swing the sign of the ECE comparison between verbalized and likelihood confidence in a majority of settings under AUROC.
lessons.excerpt: Across four QA datasets and three 7-8B Instruct models this changes which signal performs better, by point estimate, in 4 of 12 settings under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC.

lessons.point: The reordering is not a rescaling artifact — AUROC is invariant to order-preserving transforms, so the change reflects actual item reordering.
lessons.excerpt: The AUROC result cannot come from rescaling the likelihoods, since AUROC is invariant to any common order-preserving transformation; the items are ordered differently.

lessons.excerpt: replacing an accepted TriviaQA alias with the canonical reference raises confidence by $0.072$ although both answers are correct.

lessons.point: The audit finds many published comparisons omit the protocol choice entirely.
lessons.excerpt: Published comparisons diverge on this, and in a twelve-study audit five never state the choice.

entries.title: Same Attention, Different Truths: Put Logit-Lens over Visual Attention to Detect and Mitigate LVLM Object Hallucination
entries.summary: A CVPR 2026 highlight paper on object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. The authors find that real and hallucinated objects receive equally strong visual attention in mid-to-late layers, so attention magnitude is not the diagnostic. Applying Logit Lens to high-attention visual regions distinguishes them: real-object regions decode to the correct token, hallucinated ones do not. The paper decomposes hallucination into two mechanisms (visual uncertainty from confusable regions, contextual prior from co-occurrence) and proposes a training-free Detect-Mitigate framework: Logit-Lens Consistency Check for detection plus High-Attention Regions Masking (HARM) and Visual Evidence Enhanced Decoding (VEED) for mitigation.
entries.takeaway: For LVLM reliability work, attention magnitude is a weak signal because real and hallucinated targets attract comparable attention; what the attended-to features decode to under a Logit Lens is a stronger detector. This is a vision-model finding, not an agent-harness or security finding.

lessons.point: Attention magnitude does not separate real from hallucinated objects in LVLMs; both get strong attention in mid-to-late layers.
lessons.excerpt: we find that both real and hallucinated objects receive equally strong visual attention in the model's mid-to-late layers, suggesting that the key issue may not be how much the model attends, but what it attends to and why.

lessons.point: Logit Lens over high-attention visual regions provides a detection signal: real regions decode to the target token, hallucinated ones do not.
lessons.excerpt: we decode the visual features of high-attention regions using Logit Lens, and observe that regions corresponding to real objects can be correctly decoded to the target object tokens, whereas those for hallucinated objects cannot.

lessons.point: Two distinct hallucination mechanisms need different remedies: visual uncertainty is fixed by masking confusable regions; contextual prior persists after masking and requires evidence-enhanced decoding.
lessons.excerpt: (i) visual uncertainty, triggered by semantically similar or confusable regions; masking these regions eliminates the hallucination. (ii) contextual prior, triggered by strong co-occurrence priors; even when the initially attended region is masked, the hallucination persists and attention drifts to other regions.

actionable.title: News-lane only — LVLM hallucination detection, not agent security
actionable.detail: Track for interpretability-adjacent techniques (Logit Lens as a detector) that might transfer to text-only LLM hallucination or refusal analysis. No claim work — LVLM visual grounding is outside the 13-cluster scope in interests.yaml.

entries.prior_art: Logit Lens interpretability technique; prior work attributing LVLM hallucination to insufficient visual attention (this paper contests that framing).

entries.title: Semantic Adapter Routing with Fine-Tuning Task Embeddings
entries.summary: ARIADNE reframes PEFT adapter routing as classification over task embeddings and, without touching adapter weights, recovers 97.4% of Oracle task performance on 23 tasks and scales to 44 adapters at 89.7% accuracy. Its companion GRACE handles the case where training data isn't available by reconstructing an adapter's fine-tuning data from output logits alone via a modified contrastive-decoding-diffing (CDD) procedure, then using the synthesized data to build task embeddings; across three backbones (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-32B) GRACE recovers 72-100% of Oracle accuracy.
entries.takeaway: Routing at inference time can be done training-free by task-embedding-nearest-neighbor over adapters. The under-the-radar bit is GRACE: an adapter's fine-tuning data is recoverable from its output logits alone. That is a mild but real data-leakage surface for anyone who ships PEFT adapters on public hubs.

lessons.point: Adapter routing that never touches adapter weights or requires supervised training is viable at scale: 97.4% of Oracle on 23 tasks, 89.7% selection accuracy across 44 adapters.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluated on 23 tasks, ARIADNE recovers 97.4% of Oracle task performance and scales to 44 adapters at 89.7% selection accuracy, without touching a single adapter parameter.

lessons.point: Fine-tuning data can be reconstructed from an adapter's output logits alone via contrastive decoding diffing. The synthesized data is good enough to build usable task embeddings.
lessons.excerpt: GRACE, which recovers an adapter's fine-tuning data from its output logits alone via a modified contrastive decoding diffing (CDD) procedure. Synthetic data generated from CDD-UM is then used to construct task embeddings.

actionable.title: PEFT adapters on public hubs leak their training data through logits

entries.title: Calibrating WEAT Against Anisotropy: ZCA Whitening as a Geometric Pre-Processing Step for Embedding Association Tests
entries.summary: Proposes ZCA whitening as a pre-processing step for the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), which assumes an isotropic embedding space that most modern LMs do not satisfy. Across 70 model-task combinations (10 WEAT suites, 7 models), whitening reduces anisotropy, improves semantic-similarity benchmark scores for anisotropic models, and flips significance status on over 30% of WEAT results — effect sizes shift in both directions.
entries.takeaway: Bias measurements produced by WEAT on modern anisotropic embedding spaces are unreliable in both directions; prior fairness-audit numbers should be re-examined with a geometric calibration step.

lessons.point: WEAT presumes isotropy but most widely used LM embedding spaces are not isotropic.
lessons.excerpt: It relies on cosine similarity as a measure of semantic association, which assumes that the embedding space is approximately isotropic. entries.title: Seeing Is Not Deciding: Can Multimodal LLMs Act as Effective CEOs?

lessons.point: The failure mode is attributed to signal crowding: individually useful visual channels combine to disrupt constraint satisfaction during decoding, meaning visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks.

entries.title: TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation
entries.summary: TriQua proposes representing simple claims as standard subject-relation-object triples and complex claims as hyperrelational facts with auxiliary qualifiers, then verifies factuality at the level of individual triples and qualifiers. entries.title: C3PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
entries.summary: Introduces C3PO, a 3,404-sample benchmark spanning video, audio, image, and text for measuring cross-modal composition and counterfactual conflict resolution in multimodal LLMs. Reports that best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches 73.17% vs humans at 88.64%, and that 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance with attention concentrated on text.
entries.takeaway: MLLMs collapse under cross-modal conflict, defaulting to text 87-95% of the time. Not a direct security finding, but the 'modality dominance' failure mode is a candidate attack primitive worth noting for anyone deploying multimodal agents against attacker-controlled non-text inputs.

lessons.point: Multimodal models are heavily text-biased even when the ground truth lives in another modality.
lessons.excerpt: 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text.

lessons.point: Multimodal input handling is far from robust: the best frontier model still lags humans by ~15 points on this benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict.

actionable.title: Treat non-text modalities as untrusted when they conflict with text
actionable.detail: If you rely on a multimodal model to reason over image/audio/video, expect it to ignore those inputs whenever text is present. Design tests and guardrails around modality-dominance rather than assuming the model fuses evidence.

entries.prior_art: Modality bias and text dominance in MLLMs is well documented; this paper adds a counterfactual-conflict axis and quantifies attention concentration.
entries.threat: An attacker who controls a non-text modality (e.g., an image or audio clip) could rely on the model to ignore that modality when its accompanying text is benign, weakening any multimodal moderation or verification pipeline.
entries.conditions: Deployment must combine attacker-influenced non-text modality with trusted or attacker-friendly text; the paper only measures accuracy, not exploitability.
entries.mitigations: Treat cross-modal disagreement as a failure signal rather than routine; run adversarial red-team probes that pit text against other modalities; do not assume the model reads images or audio at all when text is present.

entries.title: Debias in Text, Believe Your Eyes: Text-Anchored Cross-Modal Transfer for Visual Counter-Commonsense Reasoning
entries.summary: The authors show that MLLM failures on counter-commonsense visual reasoning are not a vision-encoder problem — the correct answer is already in the decoding space — but a language-prior problem in the shared decoder. TACT is a text-only post-training framework that debiases the decoder using a fact-frequency-distilled counter-commonsense corpus, with no visual training data.
entries.takeaway: When multimodal outputs contradict the image, the fix is often at the language decoder, not the vision encoder — a text-only debiasing pass can transfer to visual reasoning.

lessons.point: MLLM counter-commonsense failures are downstream of language priors, not visual grounding: the visual evidence is already captured.
lessons.excerpt: MLLMs already capture the relevant visual evidence, and the correct answer exists in their decoding space. Instead, the shared language decoder resolves prior--evidence conflicts by favoring dominant language priors, especially for low-frequency factual scenarios.

lessons.point: A text-only post-training corpus built from fact-frequency estimates can debias a multimodal decoder without any visual training data.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce TACT, a text-anchored post-training framework that debiases the shared language decoder without requiring any visual training data.

actionable.detail: For multimodal systems, don't reflexively blame the vision path. If the model 'sees' the answer but writes something else, the language decoder is the intervention point. Diagnose which layer holds the evidence before adding training data at another.

entries.prior_art: Language-prior debiasing in VQA (VQA-CP, LMH), MLLM hallucination-reduction work (POPE, OPERA). TACT's specific contribution is text-only post-training via fact-frequency distillation; the diagnosis (decoder-side bias) is consistent with prior VQA-CP-era findings.

entries.title: ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation

entries.title: LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs
entries.summary: LUNAR is a benchmark for personalizing LLM responses from longitudinal app-interaction logs across daily-life domains (clothing, food, housing, mobility), constructed via a coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline. Across 19 LLMs, more context and larger models do not guarantee better personalization; direct retrieval of fine-grained records beats compressed memory, and stronger personalization trades off against privacy.
entries.takeaway: For personalization from long behavior logs, evidence selection and cross-domain integration matter more than raw context length or model size — and the more you personalize, the more privacy exposure you accept.

lessons.point: More context and larger models don't automatically buy better personalization from behavior logs — evidence selection and cross-domain integration are the actual levers.
lessons.excerpt: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains.

lessons.point: Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavior records outperforms compressed/summarized memory for personalization.
lessons.excerpt: Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory

lessons.point: Personalization strength trades off against privacy — you cannot maximize both simultaneously on this benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection

actionable.title: Prefer fine-grained retrieval over summarized memory when personalizing
actionable.detail: For LLM personalization from behavior logs, retrieving raw fine-grained records beat compressed memory summaries in LUNAR's evaluation — and treat privacy as an explicit knob because higher personalization strength measurably increases privacy leakage risk.

entries.prior_art: Existing personalized-LLM benchmarks based on textual personas or isolated behavior signals; retrieval-vs-summarization memory ablations in RAG literature.

entries.title: Let's Unlearn Stereotypes Before Decision-Making: Assessing the Impact of Intrinsic Bias Mitigation on Downstream Fairness in LLMs
entries.summary: Proposes Fairness-Aware Concept Unlearning (FACU), a representation-level regularizer that pushes stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical association probabilities toward parity while preserving language-model quality. Evaluated on three open LLMs and three socio-economic classification datasets; reports statistically significant intrinsic-bias drops that carry through to downstream fairness metrics, with counterfactual data augmentation stacking on top.
entries.takeaway: Bias/fairness paper, not security. Contributes evidence that intrinsic bias mitigation can meaningfully move downstream fairness metrics without tanking predictive performance — a data point for teams deploying LLMs in high-stakes classification.

lessons.point: FACU balances stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical probability differences at the representation level rather than suppressing concepts entirely.
lessons.excerpt: FACU explicitly regularizes probability differences between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical associations while preserving predictive performance and language modeling quality

lessons.point: Intrinsic gender-bias reductions were associated with downstream fairness gains across most, but not all, settings evaluated.
lessons.excerpt: FACU produces statistically significant reductions in intrinsic gender bias that are associated with downstream fairness improvements across most evaluated settings

lessons.point: Combining FACU with extrinsic mitigation (counterfactual data augmentation) yields further fairness improvements — the two approaches are complementary rather than redundant.
lessons.excerpt: Combining FACU with extrinsic mitigation methods, particularly counterfactual data augmentation, yields further fairness improvements

actionable.title: Fairness-focused unlearning is an active alignment sub-thread
actionable.detail: For any downstream product using LLM embeddings in classification of people-related features, intrinsic-plus-extrinsic bias mitigation stacking is worth an experiment slot. Not a security finding, so no threat/mitigation model applies here.
